_comment: Long-form guide copy for the tool pages, keyed by calculator id. 'what' is 2 paragraphs, 'formula' is how the maths works, 'mistakes' is a list of common errors. gen_tool_pages.py renders these under the calculator card.

everyday.what: {name} answers one of the small questions that come up every week — a percentage off a bill, a share of a total, a simple interest figure. It exists so you do not have to reach for a calculator app, a notebook and a formula you half-remember. {desc} Everything runs inside your browser, so no figure you type is sent anywhere.
everyday.formula: Every one of these tools is one arithmetic rule applied to the numbers you type. A percentage is the part divided by the whole, multiplied by 100. Simple interest is principal x rate x time. Compound interest adds the interest back to the principal at each period, so the base grows. The calculator applies the rule and shows you the result, the intermediate steps and, where it matters, the total you will actually pay or receive.
when: You are checking a shop bill or an online discount before you pay.
You are working out a share of a total — a partner's cut, a deposit, a commission.
You want a quick sanity check before you commit to a number on a form.
mistakes: Adding percentages together. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall is not back to where you started — it is 99% of it.
Using simple interest for anything longer than a year. Banks compound, so a simple-interest answer will understate what you owe.
Rounding too early. Keep the full figure and round only the answer you write down.

profit.what: {name} shows what a business actually keeps, not what it collects. Revenue is the easy number and the least useful one on its own. {desc} This tool puts the costs back in, so you can see the margin that funds the next order, the next hire and the next bad month.
profit.formula: Profit is revenue minus every cost that went into earning it. Margin is that profit divided by revenue, shown as a percentage. A 20% margin means twenty paise of every rupee of sales stays with you; the rest is eaten by goods, ads, salaries, fees and tax. Change one cost and the margin moves, which is why the tool lets you vary each line separately rather than only the total.
when: You are setting a price and want to know if the margin survives your real costs.
A month looked busy but the bank balance did not move, and you want to find out why.
You are comparing two products or two clients to decide where to put your effort.
mistakes: Counting revenue as profit. A crore of sales at a 2% margin is twenty lakh of profit — and one bad month can wipe it out.
Forgetting the costs that arrive late: GST, marketplace fees, returns, payment-gateway charges.
Setting a price by copying a competitor whose costs you cannot see.

val.what: {name} works through the arithmetic of a funding round or a company valuation. {desc} These are the numbers founders and investors argue about, and most of the arguments come down to one of the figures this tool calculates.
val.formula: Valuation is a price agreed for the whole company. Pre-money is that price before new money goes in; post-money is after. When an investor puts in an amount for a stake, the post-money is the investment divided by the stake, and the pre-money is post-money minus the investment. Revenue multiples, EBITDA multiples and implied values are different ways of arriving at the same price from the company's own numbers.
when: You are preparing for a fundraise and want to know what your numbers imply.
You have a term sheet and want to check the stake it actually gives away.
You are comparing your valuation against what similar companies raised at.
mistakes: Reading a valuation without the stake. A high valuation that costs half the company is worse than a lower one that costs a tenth.
Comparing a revenue multiple for a fast grower with one for a slow, profitable business.
Forgetting that a post-money valuation includes the new money, so the founder's percentage falls.

cust.what: {name} measures the economics of a single customer. {desc} These numbers decide whether growth makes money or burns it, and they are the first thing a serious investor checks.
cust.formula: The cost to acquire a customer (CAC) is everything you spend on sales and marketing divided by the customers it won. Lifetime value (LTV) is what one customer brings in over the whole relationship — average order value, times how often they buy, times how many years they stay, times your gross margin. Divide LTV by CAC and you have the ratio. Around 3:1 is the common rule of thumb; below 1:1 you lose money on every customer you win.
when: You are about to increase your ad budget and want to know if it will pay back.
A channel is winning customers cheaply and you want to know if that will last.
You are preparing a pitch and need the unit-economics slide.
mistakes: Using revenue for LTV instead of gross margin. The customer brings in sales, not profit.
Counting only ad spend as CAC and leaving out salaries, tools and agency fees.
Assuming a customer stays for years when your data shows most leave after a few months.

growth.what: {name} tracks the two things that kill young businesses: running out of cash, and growing faster than the cash can follow. {desc} Growth is a headline; cash is the oxygen.
growth.formula: Burn is the cash a business spends each month beyond what it earns. Runway is the cash you hold divided by that monthly burn — the number of months before the money is gone. Run rate takes one period's revenue and scales it to a year, which is useful for comparison but assumes the period repeats. Break-even is the sales level at which contribution covers your fixed costs, so profit is zero and every extra sale is profit.
when: You want to know how many months you have before you must raise or cut.
You are deciding between hiring now and waiting a quarter.
A month was unusually strong and you want to compare it fairly with the rest of the year.
mistakes: Measuring runway from revenue instead of cash in the bank.
Treating run rate as a forecast. It is a snapshot, not a promise.
Cutting the spending that wins customers first. That shortens runway now and shrinks the business later.

pricing.what: {name} works backwards from what you can charge to what you keep. {desc} Pricing is the fastest lever a small business has — a one-rupee change per unit drops straight to profit — and the one most owners set by guesswork.
pricing.formula: Start with the price the customer pays, then subtract everything between that price and your bank account: marketplace commission, shipping, packaging, payment fees, returns and discounts. What is left is your contribution. Subtract the cost of the goods and you have the profit on one unit. The tool shows each subtraction so you can see which one is doing the damage.
when: You are launching a product and need a price that leaves a real margin.
A marketplace raised its commission and you want to know how much price must move.
You are about to run a discount and want to see what it does to profit.
mistakes: Setting a price from cost plus a markup, without checking what the market will pay.
Ignoring returns. In some categories, a fifth of orders come back and the shipping is yours to pay twice.
Discounting the price without checking the extra volume needed to stand still.

ops.what: {name} prices the things a small team spends on people. {desc} The salary you agree is not the cost of the hire, and the invoice you pay is not the cost of the freelancer.
ops.formula: The full cost of an employee is the salary plus provident fund, insurance, equipment, software and the time spent managing them. For a freelancer, it is the rate times the hours, plus the hours lost to briefing and revision. Utilisation — the share of paid hours that are actually billable — is what decides whether a team makes money.
when: You are about to make a first hire and want the real monthly commitment.
You are comparing a freelancer against a full-time salary.
You want to know how many billable hours your team must sell to cover its own cost.
mistakes: Budgeting for the salary only. The full cost is often 1.2 to 1.4 times the number you agreed.
Assuming a freelancer bills every hour you pay for.
Hiring ahead of the revenue that will pay for the hire.

investor.what: {name} looks at an investment from the investor's side. {desc} Founders spend a lot of time on valuation and very little on the return the money has to earn, which is the number that actually closes a round.
investor.formula: Return on investment is the gain divided by what was put in, shown as a percentage. A multiple is the final value divided by the amount invested — 3x means you got three rupees back for every one. The annualised return converts that multiple into a yearly rate, which is the only fair way to compare a three-year exit with a ten-year one.
when: You are comparing two investments held for different lengths of time.
You are modelling what an investor needs to see for your round to make sense to them.
You are checking whether a fund's quoted return is as good as it sounds.
mistakes: Comparing multiples without the holding period. 3x in three years beats 3x in ten.
Ignoring dilution. Your multiple is on the stake you still own, not the whole company.
Treating a paper valuation as cash. It is only a return when someone buys.

bonus.what: {name} puts a pitch through the same checks an investor would run. {desc} It is a rehearsal, not a verdict — the point is to find the weak number before the meeting does.
bonus.formula: Each figure in the pitch is scored against a range that investors treat as normal: growth against what similar companies do, margin against the category, runway against the time a raise takes, and the ask against what the traction justifies. The tool combines the scores and names the lines that pull the total down.
when: You have a deck and want a second opinion before you send it.
You are practising the pitch and want to know which slide will draw questions.
You are deciding whether you are ready to raise or should wait a quarter.
mistakes: Reading a low score as a rejection. It is a list of things to fix or explain.
Tuning the inputs until the score looks good, which defeats the purpose.
Ignoring the weakest line because the total is high.

agency.what: {name} covers the economics of running client work. {desc} Agencies fail on two things: too much unbilled time, and clients who leave faster than new ones arrive.
agency.formula: Profit is the fees you bill minus the cost of delivering the work, which is mostly people's time. Utilisation is billable hours divided by available hours. Churn is the clients lost divided by the clients you started with, and a churn rate doubles as a rough measure of how long a client stays. The tool shows each of these so you can see which one is leaking.
when: You are pricing a retainer and want to know the margin before you quote.
A month felt full but the profit was thin.
You want to know how many clients you must win just to replace the ones leaving.
mistakes: Quoting a retainer from a monthly cost without allowing for unbilled revision rounds.
Treating a client as permanent. At 3% monthly churn, half are gone in under two years.
Counting total hours worked instead of billable ones.

realestate.what: {name} runs the numbers on a property purchase or a rental. {desc} Property is the largest purchase most families make, and the costs that surprise people are the ones paid on the day of registration.
realestate.formula: The cost of buying is the price plus stamp duty, registration and any brokerage. Rental yield is the annual rent divided by what the property cost, shown as a percentage. Return on a sale is the sale price minus the purchase price and costs, divided by the money you put in. A loan changes the picture: the EMI includes interest, so early payments barely reduce the principal.
when: You are comparing two properties and want to see which one earns more.
You want to know the cash you need on the day of registration, not just the price.
You are deciding between buying and continuing to rent.
mistakes: Forgetting stamp duty and registration, which together can add 6% to 8% to the price.
Comparing gross rent with the EMI. Rent is before maintenance, tax and vacancy.
Assuming prices only rise, and leaving no room for a slow year.

taxwealth.what: {name} estimates tax and long-term saving figures. {desc} The rules change, and they treat different kinds of income differently, so these tools show the arithmetic rather than a fixed answer.
taxwealth.formula: Income tax is worked out slab by slab: the rate applies only to the part of your income that falls in each band, not to the whole amount. Deductions reduce the income the slabs apply to. For savings, the future value is the amount you put in plus the interest or returns it earns, with the returns compounding if they are reinvested. The tool shows the total you contribute and the total it grows to, so you can see the split.
when: You are choosing between the old and new tax regimes.
You want to know what a monthly saving becomes over ten or twenty years.
You are checking a payslip or a Form 16 against the rules.
mistakes: Assuming a higher slab taxes all your income at that rate. It does not.
Comparing a tax-free option with a taxed one without adjusting for the tax.
Treating a projected return as guaranteed.

dailyfun.what: {name} is one of the lighter tools on the site. {desc} It is here for the fun of it — a quick answer to a question that has no bearing on your money.
dailyfun.formula: These tools follow their own published rule — a name-based pairing, a date arithmetic, a number spelled out in words. There is no financial formula involved and nothing is stored.
when: You are curious and want a quick answer.
You want to settle a friendly argument.
You are sharing something with friends.
mistakes: Making a real decision on the strength of a fun result.
Reading a fun score as advice of any kind.

agefun.what: The Age Calculator turns a date of birth into an exact age in years and months, counting the way a form or an application counts rather than the way a birthday card does. It settles whether you have completed a given number of years on today's date — the figure that decides eligibility for a school admission cut-off, a government form, a pension or an age-limited account. Because it works off today's date, it gives the age as of the day you open it, so the same birth date answers differently before and after the birthday.
agefun.formula: Age in years = today's year minus the birth year, less one if this year's birthday has not yet arrived. Age in months = 12 x years + the whole months since the last birthday. The calculator compares the day, month and year of the birth date with today's date, so it handles a February birthday and a month-end birthday correctly instead of assuming every month is thirty days.
when: You are filling a form that asks for completed years and want the exact figure, not a rounded one.
You are checking an age cut-off for a school, exam or scheme on a fixed date.
You want the exact age in years and months for a document or an application.
mistakes: Subtracting the years and ignoring whether this year's birthday has passed, which overstates the age.
Rounding up to the next birthday when the form wants completed years.
Using a rough birth-year-plus-a-bit figure for a cut-off date, where a single day decides eligibility.

agencycac.what: Client acquisition cost is what your agency spends to win one client, and it is the number that decides how much you can afford to spend on marketing. It is not just ad spend - it includes the salesperson's cost, the pitches that went nowhere, and the tools used to find and follow up leads. An agency spending ₹5 lakh a quarter to win 10 clients has a CAC of ₹50,000, and if those clients are worth ₹2 lakh over their life, the maths works.
agencycac.formula: CAC = (Marketing Spend + Sales Cost) ÷ New Clients. ₹4,00,000 of marketing and ₹1,00,000 of sales cost to win 10 clients is a CAC of ₹50,000. Compare it with client lifetime value: if LTV is ₹2,00,000, the ratio is 4 to 1, which is healthy. Below 3 to 1 the agency is spending too much to grow, and every new client makes the cash position worse before it gets better.
when: You are setting a marketing budget and want to know what a client can cost you.
You are comparing paid channels against referrals and outbound.
You are checking whether growth is actually profitable.
mistakes: Counting only ad spend and leaving the sales salary and tools out.
Dividing by all leads instead of clients actually won.
Comparing CAC with one month's fee instead of the client's full lifetime value.

agencymargin.what: Agency profit margin is what is left of your revenue after delivery and operating costs, and agencies are famous for confusing revenue with profit. A ₹1 crore agency with ₹95 lakh of costs is a ₹5 lakh business, not a ₹1 crore one. The two biggest leaks are delivery cost - the team time each client consumes - and the overhead that grows quietly as the agency does: more tools, a bigger office, more admin.
agencymargin.formula: Profit Margin % = (Revenue − Total Costs) ÷ Revenue × 100. Revenue of ₹1,00,00,000 with ₹95,00,000 of costs leaves ₹5,00,000, a 5% margin. For a services agency, 20% to 30% is healthy and 40% is excellent. The fastest fix is usually price, not cost: a 10% price rise on the same cost base takes that 5% margin to 14.5%, which no amount of tool-cutting can match.
when: You are reviewing the year and want to know what the agency actually earned.
You are setting next year's pricing and want to know the margin you need.
You are comparing a month against the same month last year.
mistakes: Calling revenue profit. The two are wildly different in an agency.
Leaving the owner's own salary out of the cost base, which flatters the margin.
Cutting tools and software when the real problem is that the work is priced too low.

agencyroas.what: ROAS is how much revenue every rupee of ad spend brought back, and it is the fastest read on whether a campaign is paying for itself. Spend Rs 1,00,000 on ads, book Rs 4,00,000 of revenue, and ROAS is 4x. What catches people out is reading 4x as profit: ROAS uses revenue, not margin, so a 4x ROAS on a product with a 20% margin is not four rupees of profit, it is eighty paise. This calculator divides ad revenue by ad spend and returns the multiple, so two channels can be compared on the same footing.
agencyroas.formula: ROAS = ad revenue / ad spend, written as a multiple such as 3x. Spend 1,00,000 and book 4,00,000 and ROAS is 4,00,000 / 1,00,000 = 4x. The tool returns that multiple alone, on purpose, because revenue is the number you can measure cleanly. To turn ROAS into a break-even test, divide 1 by your contribution margin: at a 25% margin the break-even ROAS is 1 / 0.25 = 4x, so anything below 4x loses money even while it looks profitable.
when: You are comparing two ad channels and want one number that puts them on the same scale.
A campaign is running and you want to know the spend it needs to at least break even.
You are setting a target ROAS before launch and want it grounded in your real margin.
mistakes: Reading ROAS as profit. It is revenue divided by spend, so a 4x ROAS on a thin-margin product can still lose money.
Comparing ROAS across products with different margins. Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by margin, so a 20% margin needs 5x and a 50% margin needs 2x.
Leaving out the costs outside ad spend: returns, shipping, marketplace fees and payment-gateway charges.

aov.what: Average Order Value is the typical amount a customer spends in one order. Divide total revenue by the number of orders in the same period and you have it. ₹1,00,000 across 200 orders is an AOV of ₹500. It looks like a simple average, but it drives two things: how much you can spend to acquire a customer, and how much a small nudge - a bundle, a free-shipping threshold, an upsell - is worth. Raising AOV lifts profit without spending a rupee more on ads, which makes it one of the cheapest levers a D2C brand has.
aov.formula: AOV = Total Revenue ÷ Total Orders. Use the same period for both numbers: ₹1,00,000 of revenue from 200 orders is ₹500 per order. Compare it month to month, because a rising AOV means bundles and upsells are working, while a falling one usually means discounts are eating the basket.
when: You are setting a free-shipping or bundle threshold and want a baseline.
You are measuring whether an upsell or cross-sell actually moved the basket.
You are comparing AOV across channels before deciding where to spend.
mistakes: Mixing periods - last month's revenue over this month's orders.
Letting a few very large orders skew the average without checking the median.
Confusing AOV with LTV; one order is not a customer's whole relationship.

areabreakdown.what: Built-up area versus carpet area is the quiet gap that costs Indian home buyers lakhs. Builders quote the built-up area because it is the bigger number; what you can actually put furniture on is the carpet area. The difference is called loading, and it is typically 20% to 30% for flats. A flat sold as 1,200 sq ft built-up with 25% loading has a carpet area of 900 sq ft, and the price per square foot you are really paying is a quarter higher than the brochure suggests.
areabreakdown.formula: Carpet Area = Built-up Area ÷ (1 + Loading %). A 1,200 sq ft built-up flat with 25% loading has a carpet area of 1,200 ÷ 1.25 = 960 sq ft. Flip it to see the real rate: a ₹96 lakh flat at 960 sq ft carpet costs ₹10,000 per sq ft of usable space, not the ₹8,000 the built-up figure implies. RERA requires carpet area to be disclosed, so the number on the agreement is the one to insist on.
when: You are comparing two flats and one quotes built-up while the other quotes carpet area.
You want the true per-square-foot rate on the space you can actually use.
You are checking whether the agreement matches what the brochure promised.
mistakes: Comparing a built-up area with a carpet area directly. They are not the same unit of measure.
Assuming loading is the same everywhere. It varies by builder, city and project, from under 20% to over 35%.
Forgetting that carpet area itself excludes the balcony and the external walls, so the usable space is smaller still.

ask.what: The Ask Calculator answers the question every founder has before a pitch: I need this much money, so how much equity will it cost me? Enter the amount you need and the valuation you believe the business is worth, and it shows the stake you would have to hand over. Ask for ₹45 lakh against a ₹1.8 crore valuation and you are offering a quarter of the company. The number is blunt, and that is the point - it forces a founder to ask whether the money is worth the slice before standing in front of an investor.
ask.formula: Equity to Offer = Amount Needed ÷ Valuation × 100. If you need ₹45 lakh and your valuation is ₹1.8 crore, that is ₹45,00,000 ÷ ₹1,80,00,000 × 100 = 25%. Raise the valuation and the same money costs less equity; lower it and you give away more. The formula makes the trade-off explicit, so the ask becomes a decision rather than a guess.
when: You are fixing how much to raise before a pitch.
You want to see what a bigger cheque really costs in equity.
You are comparing a small round at a high price against a large round at a low one.
mistakes: Choosing the amount you want first and the valuation second, which usually means giving away more than planned.
Comparing equity offered across deals without comparing the valuations behind them.
Forgetting that this equity is only the first round; every later round dilutes it further.

babyname.what: A baby name number calculator turns the letters of a name into a number using the same letter-values used in numerology, and shows what that number is traditionally associated with. Many Indian families look at this when choosing a name, alongside the rashi and the nakshatra. It is a tradition rather than a science, and Tank Metrics presents it that way - useful as one input among several, not as a rule.
babyname.formula: Each letter is given a value from 1 to 9 in the Chaldean or Pythagorean system, the values are added, and the digits are reduced until a single digit from 1 to 9 remains - unless the total is 11, 22 or 33, which are kept as they are. The name 'Aarav' becomes 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 6 = 11, which is one of the master numbers and is not reduced further.
when: You are choosing between two name spellings and want to compare their numbers.
You are curious what number a name reduces to.
You want a traditional input alongside the rashi and nakshatra.
mistakes: Treating the number as a hard rule for choosing a name. It is a tradition, not a requirement.
Getting different answers by spelling the name differently, and not realising the spelling is what changed the number.
Ignoring the rashi and the family's own preferences because of the number alone.

bmi.what: A BMI calculator estimates body mass index from height and weight, giving a rough indication of whether an adult is underweight, in the normal range, overweight or obese. It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis: it does not distinguish muscle from fat, and it is not designed for children, pregnant women, or very muscular people. In India the healthy range is adjusted downwards, because the risk of diabetes and heart disease rises at a lower BMI than it does in Western populations.
bmi.formula: BMI = Weight in kilograms ÷ (Height in metres)². Someone weighing 70 kg at 1.70 m: 70 ÷ (1.70 × 1.70) = 70 ÷ 2.89 = 24.2. The standard WHO ranges are under 18.5 underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 normal, 25 to 29.9 overweight and 30 plus obese. For Indians, health authorities often treat 23 as the upper end of normal, so a BMI of 24.2 is a caution rather than a clean bill of health.
when: You want a quick general indication of where your weight sits for your height.
You are tracking a change over time rather than reading a single number.
You want to know the Indian-adjusted range, which is lower than the WHO one.
mistakes: Treating BMI as a diagnosis. It is a screening estimate and misses muscle, bone density and body composition.
Using the WHO range for an Indian adult, where the healthy ceiling is lower.
Applying it to children or pregnant women, for whom BMI is not the right measure at all.

breakeven.what: A break-even point is the exact sales volume at which a business stops losing money and starts making it. Below it every sale still leaves you short of your fixed costs; at it the rent, salaries and bills are covered; above it each extra unit contributes. It is the first number a lender or an investor actually wants, because it tells them how much room there is between the business's current sales and disaster.
breakeven.formula: Break-Even Units = Fixed Costs ÷ (Selling Price − Variable Cost). Fixed costs of ₹2,00,000 a month, a product selling at ₹500 with ₹300 of variable cost, leaves ₹200 contribution per unit, so break-even is 1,000 units. In rupees that is 1,000 × ₹500 = ₹5,00,000 of revenue a month. Raise the price or cut the variable cost and the break-even falls - that is the whole lever.
when: You are setting a monthly sales target and want the floor, not the aspiration.
You are deciding whether to take on fixed costs like a shop or a hire.
A lender or investor has asked how much you need to sell to stop losing money.
mistakes: Leaving some fixed costs out of the calculation, which makes break-even look far closer than it is.
Using gross revenue instead of contribution - what matters is what each unit leaves after its own variable cost.
Treating break-even as a profit target. At break-even you make nothing; it is the point where the losses stop.

breakevenad.what: Break-even ad spend is the most you can pay for advertising before a campaign stops making money. It is the ceiling, not a target, and it is set by your own margin - not by what competitors bid or what a platform suggests. A product with ₹300 of contribution per sale can afford to spend almost all of that to win the sale and still break even, but every rupee above it is a loss. Knowing this number stops you from bidding your way into a loss.
breakevenad.formula: Contribution per Sale = Revenue per Sale − Product Cost per Sale. Break-Even Ad Spend = Contribution per Sale × Expected Conversions. Sell at ₹1,000 with a product cost of ₹600 and the contribution is ₹400. Expecting 20 conversions, you can spend up to ₹8,000 and break even - an ₹8,000 ad budget, or a maximum cost per acquisition of ₹400. Spend ₹10,000 and the campaign loses ₹2,000.
when: You are setting a maximum bid or a daily ad budget.
A campaign is running and you want to know when to switch it off.
You are comparing two products and want to see which can support more ad spend.
mistakes: Using revenue instead of contribution. The product cost has to come out before ad spend is affordable.
Treating break-even as the target. At break-even you make nothing; you need to spend below it.
Forgetting delivery, packaging and payment fees, which reduce the contribution and therefore the ceiling.

brokerage.what: A brokerage calculator works out the commission payable to a property agent, whether on a sale or on a rental agreement. In India the rate is negotiable and varies by city and by property value - commonly 1% to 2% of the transaction value on a sale, and one month's rent on a rental, split between landlord and tenant. On a ₹1.2 crore flat at 1%, the brokerage is ₹1.2 lakh, and it is payable at the time of the deal, not out of the loan.
brokerage.formula: Brokerage = Transaction Amount × Commission Rate. A ₹1.2 crore sale at 1% is ₹1,20,000. For a rental, brokerage is usually one month's rent, so a ₹35,000 a month flat costs ₹35,000, often shared equally between landlord and tenant. On high-value deals the percentage is negotiable downwards - a 2% rate on a ₹5 crore property is ₹10 lakh, and most agents will discuss that.
when: You are buying or selling and want to know the commission before you agree to it.
You are renting and want to check what the agent is asking against the norm.
You are comparing two agents quoting different rates.
mistakes: Assuming the rate is fixed. Brokerage in India is negotiable and varies widely by city.
Forgetting that brokerage cannot be added to the home loan - it is cash, paid at the deal.
Paying on both sides without checking the agreement. On a rental, the standard is one month's rent in total, not one month from each side.

burn.what: Burn rate is how fast a business spends its cash each month; runway is how many months are left before the money runs out. Put ₹10,00,000 in the bank against a ₹1,00,000 monthly burn and you have ten months. Both numbers are estimates of a future you can still change, which is the point: a founder who knows the runway in March can cut costs in March, and one who finds out in December cannot. Runway is the single number that decides how long you have to make the plan work.
burn.formula: Runway (months) = Cash in Bank ÷ Net Monthly Burn. Net burn is monthly expenses minus monthly income - if the business already earns more than it spends, there is no burn and the runway is unlimited. ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 10 months. Recalculate every month, because both the cash and the burn move.
when: You are planning how long a fundraise has to close.
You are deciding whether to hire now or wait.
You are reporting to investors and need the cash position in one line.
mistakes: Using gross burn (expenses) instead of net burn (expenses minus income), which understates the runway.
Forgetting one-off costs - a tax bill, a big renewal - that lands inside the runway window.
Treating runway as fixed; it changes the moment revenue or spend changes, so it must be recalculated monthly.

cac.what: Customer Acquisition Cost is the rupee figure behind one question: what did it cost to win a single customer? Add up everything you spent on ads, sales salaries, agency fees and discounts in a period, divide by the number of new customers that spend brought in, and you have your CAC. It is the first number a founder should know, because it decides whether growth adds cash or burns it. Spend ₹1,00,000 to win 200 customers and each one cost ₹500 - cheap or expensive only next to what that customer is worth.
cac.formula: CAC = Total Sales and Marketing Spend ÷ New Customers Won. Count the whole cost of winning a customer - ad spend, the sales team, agency fees, introductory discounts - over a fixed period, then divide by the new customers added in that same period. ₹1,00,000 of spend that brings 200 new customers is a CAC of ₹500. If you leave out salaries or discounts, the number flatters you and the real cost stays hidden.
when: You are about to scale ad spend and want the cost per customer before you commit the budget.
An investor asks whether your growth is efficient, and you need one number to answer.
You are comparing two channels - a cheap-looking one with a high CAC often loses to a costlier one with a low CAC.
mistakes: Counting only ad spend and leaving out sales salaries, agency fees and tooling, so the CAC looks far lower than it is.
Dividing this month's spend by last month's customers, which mixes two periods and gives a number that means nothing.
Comparing CAC to revenue instead of to gross profit - you repay the cost of a customer out of profit, not turnover.

cagr.what: CAGR is the single steady yearly rate that would take a business from where it started to where it ended, ignoring how bumpy the ride was. It is the fairest way to describe growth because it does not care whether the growth came evenly or in one good year. A business going from ₹1 crore to ₹2.5 crore in four years has grown at roughly 25.7% a year, even if it did nothing in year one and doubled in year four. Investors ask for CAGR because it makes two businesses comparable.
cagr.formula: CAGR = (Ending Value ÷ Starting Value)^(1 ÷ Years) − 1. ₹1 crore to ₹2.5 crore over 4 years: (2.5)^(1/4) − 1 = 25.7% a year. The same ₹1 crore to ₹2.5 crore in 2 years is 58.1% a year - the same outcome, a very different business. That is why a CAGR without a time period attached is meaningless.
when: You are reporting growth to an investor and want a single honest yearly number.
You are comparing your growth with a competitor's over different periods.
You are checking whether a projected growth rate is realistic for your business stage.
mistakes: Using simple average growth instead of CAGR. Averaging a good year and a bad year gives a number that never actually happened.
Quoting a CAGR over too short a period. Two years of high growth says very little about a business.
Applying CAGR to a number that swung wildly. It smooths the path, which can flatter a business that had one exceptional year.

captable.what: A cap table is the running list of who owns what: founders, investors, and the employee option pool. This tool takes the ESOP pool and the investor stake and shows what the founders keep. Set aside an 18% option pool and 18% for investors and the founders hold 64%. The cap table is where dilution stops being a feeling and becomes a number, and it is the first document a serious investor asks to see - a messy one reads as a founder who has not done the work.
captable.formula: Founders' Share = 100% − ESOP Pool − Investor Equity (and any other reserved stake). 100% − 18% − 18% = 64%. Every row on the cap table is a percentage of the same whole, so the rows must add to 100; if they do not, something is double-counted or missing.
when: You are preparing a data room for a fundraise.
You are sizing an ESOP pool before hiring senior staff.
You want to check a term sheet against your current table.
mistakes: Sizing the ESOP pool after the round instead of before, so founders absorb more dilution than planned.
Leaving out convertible notes or SAFEs, which convert later and dilute the table unexpectedly.
Letting the percentages not add to 100, which hides a missing holder.

ccc.what: The cash conversion cycle is how many days your money is stuck in the business between paying for stock and getting paid by customers. A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash, and this is usually why. You buy inventory, hold it, sell it on credit, and only then collect. Every day in that chain is a day your money is working for someone else. Cutting the cycle is often faster than growing sales.
ccc.formula: CCC = Days Inventory + Days Receivables − Days Payables. If stock sits for 60 days, customers take 45 days to pay, and you pay suppliers in 30 days, the cycle is 60 + 45 − 30 = 75 days. That means 75 days of costs have to be funded from somewhere - usually your own pocket or a loan. Negotiating 45-day supplier terms instead of 30 cuts the cycle to 60 days with no extra sales at all.
when: You are profitable but constantly short of cash and want to see where it is stuck.
You are negotiating payment terms with a supplier or a large customer.
You are planning how much working capital you need before the busy season.
mistakes: Measuring the cycle on the best customer and not the average one. One slow payer can carry the whole number.
Extending payables to improve the ratio without noticing that suppliers then raise prices or stop supplying.
Confusing profit with cash. A profitable business with a 90-day cycle can still fail.

churn.what: Churn rate is the percentage of clients or customers you lose in a period, and it is the number that quietly decides whether a business grows or runs to stand still. Losing 5% of clients a month does not sound serious until you realise it means losing almost half of them in a year. Churn also caps your growth: if you lose 8 clients a month and win 8, you are working hard to stay exactly where you are.
churn.formula: Churn Rate % = Clients Lost ÷ Clients at Start × 100. Losing 6 of 120 clients is 5% monthly churn. Annualised, roughly 46% of the base is gone in a year. To actually grow by 10 clients a month you must win 16, because 6 are leaving. Reducing churn from 5% to 3% is often worth more than doubling new sales, and it is cheaper, because the clients are already yours.
when: You are reviewing client retention and want the honest monthly figure.
You are setting a sales target and need to know how much of it churn will eat.
You are deciding whether to invest in retention or acquisition.
mistakes: Measuring churn yearly and missing that the monthly figure compounds.
Counting a client as retained because the contract exists, even though they have stopped using the service.
Reporting revenue churn when the question was customer churn - one large client leaving moves the two very differently.

clientltv.what: Client lifetime value is the total revenue one client brings you before they leave, and for an agency it is the number that decides how much you can afford to spend winning them. A client paying ₹40,000 a month who stays 18 months is worth ₹7.2 lakh - not ₹40,000. Agencies that price, hire and advertise as if every client is worth one month's fee are permanently cash-starved, because they are spending as though the relationship is a one-off when it is actually a year-and-a-half annuity.
clientltv.formula: LTV = Monthly Revenue × Average Lifetime in months. ₹40,000 a month for 18 months is ₹7.2 lakh. For a truer figure, use gross margin instead of revenue: at a 60% margin the same client is worth ₹4.32 lakh of actual profit. The ratio that matters is LTV against the cost of acquiring the client - a healthy agency aims for LTV at three times CAC or better.
when: You are setting a retainer price and want to know what the relationship is actually worth.
You are deciding how much you can pay for a lead or an outbound campaign.
You are comparing two client types and want to know which is worth more over a year, not a month.
mistakes: Using revenue and calling it value. Margin is what you keep, and a high-revenue client with heavy delivery cost can be the least valuable one you have.
Guessing the average lifetime instead of measuring it. Most agencies overestimate how long clients stay by a wide margin.
Ignoring churn. If a quarter of clients leave each year, the average lifetime is four years, not forever.

clientprofit.what: Client profitability answers the question an agency owner asks too late: after paying the team, the tools and the overhead, did this client actually make me money? A ₹2 lakh a month retainer feels like a good client until you count the three people on it, the ad tools, and the share of rent and admin it consumes. Many agencies discover their biggest client is their thinnest margin, and their smallest is quietly the most profitable. This calculator puts the delivery cost and the overhead next to the fee.
clientprofit.formula: Client Profit = Fee − Delivery Cost − Allocated Overhead. Margin % = (Profit ÷ Fee) × 100. A ₹2,00,000 fee with ₹1,30,000 of delivery cost and ₹30,000 of allocated overhead leaves ₹40,000, a 20% margin. For agencies, 40% to 60% is healthy, 20% is fragile, and below 15% the client is usually one late payment away from being a loss. The point of the exercise is to find the clients to raise prices for, not to fire them.
when: You are reviewing the client list and want to see which relationships actually pay.
You are about to renew a retainer and want the numbers before you agree a price.
You are deciding whether to take on a new client at the price they are offering.
mistakes: Leaving overhead out. Rent, software and admin are real costs and every client carries a share of them.
Counting only the hours you can see. An agency owner's own time is a cost even when it is not on a timesheet.
Firing the low-margin client before trying a price increase. Often the fix is a higher fee, not a lost client.

cm.what: Contribution margin is what is left from each sale after the variable cost of making it, and it is the number that tells you whether a product can pay for the business at all. Sell at Rs 500 with Rs 300 of variable cost and the contribution is Rs 200, a 40% margin. That Rs 200 is what covers rent, salaries, ads and every other fixed cost; only once the fixed costs are covered does any of it become profit. This calculator takes your selling price and variable cost per unit and returns the contribution per unit and as a percentage, so you can see how many units it takes to break even.
cm.formula: Contribution margin per unit = selling price - variable cost per unit. As a percentage, divide that by the selling price: (selling price - variable cost) / selling price x 100. At a price of 500 and a variable cost of 300 the contribution is 500 - 300 = 200, which is 200 / 500 x 100 = 40%. Fixed costs do not enter this calculation at all; they are what the contribution has to cover, and the break-even point is fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit.
when: You are deciding whether a product is worth selling at all, before you look at fixed costs.
You are setting a discount and want to know how far the price can fall before the contribution disappears.
You are choosing between two products to push and want to compare them on what each sale contributes, not on revenue.
mistakes: Folding fixed costs into the variable cost. Rent and salaries are fixed; only materials, packaging and per-order fees are variable.
Confusing contribution margin with net margin. Contribution ignores fixed costs, so it is always the larger number.
Discounting by the contribution percentage rather than the price. A 20% cut on a 40% contribution margin removes half the contribution, not a fifth of it.

codrto.what: The COD & RTO Loss Calculator puts a rupee figure on the cash-on-delivery orders that come back. RTO — return to origin — is the parcel a courier carries to the customer, fails to deliver, and brings back to you; you pay the forward freight, the return freight and often the packaging, and you never make the sale. The tool turns your COD volume and RTO rate into the number of parcels that bounce and the money those bounces take out of the month. Open it when a category looks profitable on paper but the bank balance disagrees, because RTO is the cost that never appears in a margin sheet until it is added by hand.
codrto.formula: RTO orders = total COD orders x RTO rate / 100. Total loss = RTO orders x loss per RTO order. Loss per RTO order is the all-in cost of one bounce — forward freight plus return freight plus packaging plus any re-attempt charge — not just the courier bill you see first. The tool multiplies the two so you can watch the loss scale with volume.
when: Your COD share is high and you want to know what the returns cost before you cut it.
You are deciding whether a prepaid discount is worth moving customers off COD.
You are negotiating freight rates and want to show the courier what RTO is costing you.
mistakes: Counting only the return freight and forgetting the forward leg, which you pay either way.
Treating RTO as a share of all orders rather than of COD orders, which understates it.
Ignoring the second sale a returned parcel kills, since the stock sits out of the market for a week.

cofounder.what: Co-founder equity split answers the hardest conversation in an early startup: who gets how much. The fairest approach scores each founder on what they actually bring - the idea, capital, time, skills, network and risk taken - and divides the equity in proportion to those scores. Enter each founder's score and the calculator gives the percentage. An equal 12-12-12 gives a clean three-way split, but most real splits are not equal, and putting the reasons into numbers now prevents a fight later when the company is worth something.
cofounder.formula: Founder Share % = Founder Score ÷ Total of All Scores × 100. Three founders scoring 12, 12 and 12 hold 33.3% each; scores of 20, 15 and 10 give 44.4%, 33.3% and 22.2%. Score what each person is contributing - money, full-time commitment, the idea, the skills - so the split reflects work rather than who spoke first.
when: You and your co-founders are setting up the cap table for the first time.
A new co-founder joins and the existing split must be redone.
An investor asks why the founding equity is divided the way it is.
mistakes: Splitting equally to avoid an argument, then resenting it when one founder does most of the work.
Giving the idea the largest share and the person who will actually run the business a smaller one.
Leaving the split in chat messages instead of a signed agreement with vesting.

compatibility.what: A compatibility calculator compares two names with a playful scoring formula and returns a percentage. It is the same idea as the love calculator with a different method - letters are matched, counted and reduced to a score. There is no claim behind it and no evidence for it. It is a fun tool, and the site says so plainly rather than dressing it up as insight.
compatibility.formula: The two names are matched letter by letter, common letters are counted and weighted, and the total is reduced to a percentage out of 100. The same pair of names always produces the same result, which is the only predictable thing about it. A high score is no more meaningful than a low one - both are arithmetic on letters.
when: You want a quick, playful answer to share.
You are curious how two names score against each other.
You want a light-hearted tool, not an assessment.
mistakes: Reading the score as a real measure of compatibility between people.
Drawing any conclusion about a relationship from it.
Assuming a different spelling would not change the answer - it would.

compint.what: Compound Interest works out what an amount grows to when the interest is added back and earns interest itself. ₹10,000 at 8% for five years is not ₹14,000; it is more, because each year's interest joins the balance. The tool also takes how many times a year the interest compounds, which is the part most people miss: the same rate paid monthly ends higher than the same rate paid once a year.
compint.formula: Total = Principal × (1 + Rate ÷ Times ÷ 100) ^ (Times × Years). Rate is the yearly percentage, Times is how often interest is added in a year (1, 4 or 12), and Years is the term. The tool subtracts the principal from the total to show the interest earned on its own. Raising the Times figure raises the total for the same headline rate.
when: You are comparing a fixed deposit that compounds quarterly with one that compounds monthly.
You are projecting what a monthly SIP or a lump sum grows to over several years.
You want to see how much of a long loan's total cost is interest rather than principal.
mistakes: Using simple interest for a multi-year figure. Banks compound, so a simple-interest answer always understates what you will owe or earn.
Ignoring how often it compounds. 8% paid monthly is not the same as 8% paid yearly, and the gap widens with the term.
Forgetting that the rate is annual. Entering a monthly rate in the yearly field multiplies the answer by twelve times over.

cpcpa.what: A CPC to CPA converter takes what you pay for a click and turns it into what you pay to actually acquire a customer. CPC is the price of a visit; CPA is the price of a result. The bridge between them is your conversion rate, and it is usually the cheapest thing to improve. At a ₹10 CPC and a 2% conversion rate, a customer costs ₹500. Improve the conversion rate to 4% and the same customer costs ₹250 - with no change in the ad, the audience or the bid.
cpcpa.formula: CPA = CPC ÷ Conversion Rate. ₹10 per click at 2% conversion gives ₹500 per acquisition. The same ₹10 at 5% gives ₹200. Flip it to set a target: if you can afford ₹300 per customer at a 3% conversion rate, you can bid up to ₹9 per click. That single division is how you decide a bid instead of guessing at it.
when: You know your CPC and conversion rate and want the true cost of a customer.
You are setting a maximum bid from the CPA you can afford.
You are deciding whether to spend more on traffic or on making the landing page convert better.
mistakes: Treating CPC as the cost of a customer. It is the cost of a visit, and most visits do not buy.
Improving the ad when the landing page is what loses the sale. Conversion rate is where the leverage usually is.
Using a blended conversion rate when mobile and desktop behave completely differently.

cpmcpc.what: A CPM to CPC converter turns what you paid for a thousand impressions into what you actually paid for one click. CPM is how ad platforms sell inventory - the price per thousand views. CPC is what that costs you in practice once real people start clicking. The gap between the two is your click-through rate, and it is the single number that decides whether a campaign is cheap or expensive. Two campaigns can both be quoted at ₹200 CPM and deliver wildly different CPCs, because one creative gets clicked and the other does not.
cpmcpc.formula: CPC = (CPM ÷ 1000) × Impressions ÷ Clicks, which simplifies to CPM ÷ (CTR% × 10). At ₹200 CPM with 50,000 impressions and 1,000 clicks: spend is ₹10,000, so CPC is ₹10. Double the click-through rate to 4% and the CPC halves to ₹5 with no change in CPM. That is why a better creative is usually worth more than a bigger budget - it lowers the price of every click you buy.
when: A platform quotes you a CPM and you want to know the real cost per click before you commit budget.
Two channels look similarly priced on CPM and you want to compare them on CPC.
You are setting a target CPC and working backwards to the click-through rate you need.
mistakes: Comparing CPM across platforms as if it were the final cost. It is the entry price, not the outcome.
Reading a low CPC as good without checking the quality of the clicks. Cheap clicks that never convert are the most expensive kind.
Forgetting that CPM is per thousand impressions, not per impression, which throws the arithmetic off by a factor of 1,000.

ctc.what: A CTC calculator shows what an employee actually costs the company, which is always more than the salary in the offer letter. On top of gross salary the employer pays provident fund, and often gratuity, insurance and other benefits. For a small business owner this is the number to budget, because hiring at ₹50,000 a month costs meaningfully more than ₹50,000 a month. For an employee it explains why take-home is smaller than the CTC.
ctc.formula: Employer Cost = Gross Monthly Salary + Employer PF + Other Monthly Benefits, and the yearly figure is twelve times that. A ₹50,000 gross salary with a 12% employer PF of ₹6,000 and ₹2,000 of other benefits costs ₹58,000 a month, or ₹6,96,000 a year. Add gratuity at roughly 4.81% of basic and the true annual cost crosses ₹7 lakh - against a CTC that looked like ₹6 lakh.
when: You are hiring and want the real monthly cost to budget for.
You are an employee checking why take-home is much lower than CTC.
You are comparing a full-time hire against a freelancer.
mistakes: Budgeting only the gross salary and being surprised by the PF and benefits cost.
Confusing CTC with take-home. CTC includes employer contributions that never reach the employee's bank account.
Forgetting gratuity, which accrues every year and is payable at the end of service.

daysbetween.what: Days between two dates counts the calendar days from one date to another, which sounds trivial until you need it. It is used to work out notice periods, invoice due dates, interest accrual, project timelines and the days left before a deadline. It counts calendar days, not working days, so a 30-day notice period spans weekends and holidays too - which is why a 'one-month' notice is often more than 30 days.
daysbetween.formula: Days = End Date − Start Date, counted as calendar days. From 1 April to 30 April is 29 days, not 30, because the start date is not counted. From 15 January to 15 March in a non-leap year is 59 days. For a due date, add the credit period to the invoice date: a 45-day term on a 1 March invoice falls due on 15 April.
when: You are checking a notice period or a contract deadline.
You are working out when an invoice actually falls due.
You are planning a project timeline and need the number of days.
mistakes: Counting the start date as day one, which adds a day to every answer.
Confusing calendar days with working days. Only the first includes weekends and holidays.
Forgetting that February changes length in a leap year, which shifts every date after it.

debteq.what: A debt-plus-equity deal splits the money an investor puts in into two parts: a loan the business must repay, and equity that buys a permanent stake. It is common on Shark Tank India because it lets a shark take less ownership while still getting the cash back. Enter the total deal, the debt portion and the valuation for the equity part, and you see the loan amount, the equity amount and the stake it buys. The debt is repaid from cash flow whether or not the business grows; the equity is never repaid at all.
debteq.formula: Debt Amount = Total Deal × Debt Portion %; Equity Amount = Total Deal − Debt Amount; Equity % = Equity Amount ÷ Valuation × 100. On a ₹4.5 crore deal with 18% as debt, ₹81 lakh is a loan and the rest buys equity at the agreed valuation. The debt is a fixed obligation, the equity a permanent claim - mixing them hides which one is actually expensive.
when: A term sheet mixes a loan with equity and you want each part separated.
You are deciding how much of a deal to take as repayable debt rather than permanent equity.
You are comparing a pure-equity offer against one with a debt component.
mistakes: Treating the whole deal as equity and undercounting the dilution.
Forgetting the debt portion must be repaid from cash flow, which squeezes working capital.
Judging the deal on the stake alone when the debt is what decides whether the business can breathe.

depreciation.what: Straight-line depreciation spreads the cost of an asset evenly across the years you expect to use it. A machine costing ₹10 lakh that will last ten years costs the business ₹1 lakh a year, whether or not you spend anything that year. It is not a cash payment - it is the accounting way of matching the cost of the asset to the years that benefit from it, and it is what makes the profit figure honest.
depreciation.formula: Yearly Depreciation = (Asset Cost − Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life. A ₹10,00,000 machine with a ₹1,00,000 resale value over 10 years depreciates at (10,00,000 − 1,00,000) ÷ 10 = ₹90,000 a year. After four years the book value is ₹10,00,000 − ₹3,60,000 = ₹6,40,000. For tax, the Income Tax Act uses written-down value blocks instead, so the accounting figure and the tax figure differ - your accountant reconciles the two.
when: You are preparing accounts and need the yearly charge for an asset.
You are comparing buying equipment against renting it, and the true yearly cost matters.
You want to know what an asset is still worth on the books.
mistakes: Treating depreciation as cash leaving the business. It is a non-cash charge and the money was spent when you bought the asset.
Using a useful life that is too long to make profits look better - the asset then breaks before it is written off.
Forgetting that tax depreciation follows the Income Tax Act's rates, not your own estimate.

dilution.what: Dilution is the slice of the company a founder gives up in a deal, and the slice that is left. If you own 100% today and hand an investor 10%, you keep 90% - but the number that matters is what that 10% buys. Dilution compounds: a 10% round, then a 20% round, then an ESOP pool, and a founder who started at 100% can end up below half. This calculator shows the ownership after a single round, so the cost of a deal is visible before it is signed, not after.
dilution.formula: Founder Equity After = Founder Equity Before − Equity Offered. 100% − 10% = 90%. Across several rounds, multiply the fractions rather than subtracting the percentages: 90% after round one, then a further 20% off leaves 72%, not 70%. The multiplication is why dilution surprises founders - each round is charged against a smaller base.
when: You have a term sheet and want to see your ownership after the stake.
You are planning two rounds and want to know where you land.
You are setting an ESOP pool and need to see its effect on founders.
mistakes: Subtracting percentages across rounds instead of multiplying fractions, which understates the loss.
Forgetting the ESOP pool, which dilutes founders exactly like an investor does.
Looking at the stake alone without the valuation - giving 20% at a high price can cost less than 5% at a low one.

discountimpact.what: A discount impact calculator shows what a discount actually costs you, and it is far more than the percentage suggests. A 10% discount on a product with a 40% margin does not cost you 10% of profit - it costs you a quarter of it. This is the number founders miss when they offer a 'small' discount to close a deal, because the discount comes off the price while the cost stays exactly where it was.
discountimpact.formula: New Price = Selling Price × (1 − Discount %). New Profit = New Price − Cost Price. A product selling at ₹1,000 with a cost of ₹600 has ₹400 profit. A 10% discount takes the price to ₹900, so profit falls to ₹300 - a 25% drop in profit for a 10% discount. To earn back the lost profit you would need 33% more sales volume, which is why blanket discounts are so rarely worth it.
when: A customer asks for a discount and you want to know what it really costs.
You are running a sale and want the volume you need just to break even on it.
You are comparing a discount against other ways to win the sale.
mistakes: Reading the discount as a percentage of profit. It comes off the price, and profit is a much smaller number.
Giving the discount without working out the extra volume it needs to justify itself.
Discounting a low-margin product, where the same percentage wipes out most or all of the profit.

distmargin.what: Distributor and retailer margin calculator shows how the difference between what you sell at and what the customer pays is split down the chain. In India a physical product usually moves manufacturer to distributor to retailer to customer, and each stage needs enough margin to keep the product on the shelf. If you set the MRP without checking each stage, the product simply does not get pushed - distributors and retailers quietly prefer the brand that pays them more. This calculator shows the margin at every step.
distmargin.formula: Distributor Margin % = (MRP − Distributor Price) ÷ MRP × 100, and Retailer Margin % = (Distributor Price − Manufacturer Price) ÷ Distributor Price × 100, depending on which stage is being measured. Typical ranges in India: distributor 8% to 12%, retailer 15% to 25%. If your product costs ₹60 to make and the MRP is ₹100, there is ₹40 to share. Giving the distributor 10% and the retailer 20% leaves ₹30 to you, and that is your real margin.
when: You are launching a physical product and need to set an MRP that leaves everyone a margin.
A distributor says your margins are too thin and you want to check whether they are right.
You are comparing selling direct online against going through the trade.
mistakes: Setting the MRP from your own cost without leaving room for the trade, then wondering why nobody stocks it.
Calculating margins on the wrong base - distributor margin is usually on MRP, retailer margin on the price they buy at.
Forgetting that GST sits on top of all of this and is not part of anyone's margin.

downpayment.what: A down payment calculator tells you the cash you must arrange before a home loan starts, and it is the number that stops most first-time buyers. Banks in India typically lend 75% to 90% of the property value, so the remaining 10% to 25% has to come from your own pocket. On a ₹80 lakh flat at an 80% loan-to-value, the down payment is ₹16 lakh - and that is before stamp duty and registration, which cannot be borrowed at all.
downpayment.formula: Down Payment = Property Price × (1 − Loan-to-Value %). A ₹80 lakh flat at 80% LTV needs ₹16 lakh down and a ₹64 lakh loan. The cash you actually need on day one is larger: add stamp duty and registration, usually 6% to 8%, so about ₹5 lakh more, making it ₹21 lakh. Lenders set the LTV from the lower of the agreement value and the valuation report, so a high quoted price does not always raise the loan.
when: You have picked a property and need to know the cash to arrange before applying.
You are comparing two flats and one needs far more upfront than the other.
You are working out how much you need to save before you can buy.
mistakes: Budgeting only the down payment and forgetting stamp duty and registration, which add several lakh on a typical flat.
Assuming the bank will fund the full property price. The LTV cap is on the valuation, not the asking price.
Draining your entire savings for the down payment and leaving nothing for registration, shifting costs or an emergency.

ebitda.what:
EBITDA & Margin answers the question an investor asks before any other: does this business make money from the thing it actually does? The tool takes revenue, strips out the cost of the goods sold and the operating expenses that keep the lights on, and shows what is left — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — together with that figure as a percentage of revenue. The rupee number says how much the core operation throws off; the margin says how efficiently it does it.

The margin is the part that travels. Two firms can report the same ₹10 lakh of EBITDA and be in completely different health: ₹10 lakh on ₹50 lakh of revenue is a 20% margin and a business with pricing power, while ₹10 lakh on ₹5 crore of revenue is a 2% margin and a business one bad month from a loss. Because it stops before interest and tax, EBITDA also lets you compare a debt-free company with a heavily borrowed one on the same footing — which is exactly why lenders and buyers reach for it.
ebitda.formula: EBITDA = Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold − Operating Expenses. The margin is EBITDA ÷ Revenue × 100, and the tool shows it beside the rupee figure. Revenue is the top line (rev), Cost of Goods Sold is cogs and Operating Expenses is opex. Interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation are deliberately left out, so EBITDA is not the cash you keep — it is the profit from running the business, before financing and accounting decisions. A margin above 15% is usually treated as attractive; below 5% there is little room for a bad quarter.
when: You are showing a business to an investor and want one clean number for core profitability.
You are comparing two companies that are funded in completely different ways.
You want to check for yourself whether the operation still earns in a bad month, before interest and tax flatter or hide it.
mistakes: Treating revenue as EBITDA. ₹5 crore of sales at a 2% margin leaves only ₹10 lakh, and one weak month can erase it.
Feeding interest and tax into the operating costs. They are financing and tax charges, not trading costs, and including them understates the margin.
Judging the margin from a single quarter. One-off costs and seasonality move it around; the trend is what to trust.

ebitdamul.what: The EBITDA Multiple divides a valuation by EBITDA — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. It is the multiple most small-business deals are actually priced on, because it ignores how the current owner financed the business and how the accountant spread the cost of equipment. Two identical shops with different loans and different depreciation policies show the same EBITDA, so the multiple compares like with like.
ebitdamul.formula: EBITDA Multiple = Valuation ÷ EBITDA. The tool divides the valuation you enter by the EBITDA figure and shows the result in times. A 6x multiple means the buyer pays six rupees for every one rupee of yearly operating profit. Because EBITDA is a profit measure and revenue is not, this multiple is always lower than the revenue multiple for the same deal.
when: You are selling or buying a business and want a price that a lender or an investor will recognise as normal.
You are comparing an offer against the 4-8x range most small business deals fall in.
You want to check what EBITDA the business must reach for the asking price to be reasonable.
mistakes: Adding back costs that are real. A one-off saving the owner made by not paying himself is not a permanent add-back, and buyers discount it.
Comparing an EBITDA multiple to a revenue multiple. They measure different things; a 6x EBITDA price is not 'cheaper' than a 3x revenue price without the margin between them.
Using a stale EBITDA. One good year lifts the multiple's denominator and makes an average business look cheap.

emi.what: The Loan EMI Calculator shows what a loan really costs per month and over its whole life. The EMI is the fixed amount you pay every month; it contains both interest and a repayment of the amount borrowed. Early payments are almost all interest, which is why a loan feels like it is not shrinking for the first few years.
emi.formula: The EMI is calculated so that every payment, compounded at the monthly rate over the full term, exactly clears the loan. The monthly rate is the annual rate divided by twelve, and the term is the number of months. Total interest is the EMI multiplied by the number of months, minus the amount borrowed. A longer term lowers the EMI but raises the total interest, which is the trade the calculator lets you test.
when: You are comparing two loan offers with different rates or terms.
You want to know the monthly payment before you commit to a property.
You are deciding whether a longer term is worth the extra interest.
mistakes: Choosing the offer with the lowest EMI without checking the total interest.
Forgetting the processing fee and insurance, which are added to the cost of borrowing.
Assuming the rate is fixed for the whole term when it is linked to a benchmark that moves.
emi.intro: Take a home loan of ₹30,00,000 at 8.5% over 20 years. Here is what the bank works out.
emi.outro: Notice that the total interest is close to the amount borrowed. On a long loan, the interest is not a small add-on — it is nearly a second property.

epf.what: An EPF calculator adds up the money that quietly builds in your Employees' Provident Fund account every month and shows what it becomes by the time you retire. Two people pay into it - you and your employer - and both contributions earn interest, which is where the surprise comes from. The employee share is 12% of basic salary, the employer puts in a matching amount, and the balance compounds year after year. A person who joins at 25 and retires at 58 has paid in for 33 years, and in the last ten of those the interest alone earns more than the first twenty years of contributions.
epf.formula: Yearly addition = (Employee Monthly PF + Employer Monthly PF) × 12, and the balance grows at the EPF rate compounded annually. If you and your employer together put in ₹10,000 a month at 8.25%, then after 30 years the corpus is roughly ₹1.42 crore, of which only about ₹36 lakh is money you actually paid in. The rest is compound interest, and that gap is the entire reason to start early rather than to contribute more later.
when: You want to know what your PF becomes by retirement, before deciding how much more to save elsewhere.
You are switching jobs and want to see what leaving the balance untouched actually earns.
You are comparing PF against NPS, PPF or an equity SIP on a like-for-like basis.
mistakes: Adding only your own contribution and forgetting the employer share, which roughly doubles the money going in.
Assuming the interest rate stays fixed. The EPF rate is reviewed every year and has moved between about 8% and 8.5% for a decade.
Ignoring the EPS split - part of the employer's share goes to pension rather than to the PF balance that earns interest.

exitcalc.what: An exit calculator shows what a founder or an angel investor actually walks away with when a company is sold. The headline number in the news is the company's price; the number that reaches your bank account is your equity percentage of it, and the two are very different. If you own 18% of a company that sells for ₹4.5 crore, your payout is ₹81 lakh - not ₹4.5 crore. Founders spend years arguing about valuation and almost no time on the cap table, which is the document that decides this number on the day it matters.
exitcalc.formula: Payout = Exit Valuation × Your Equity %. A 12% stake in a ₹25 crore sale pays ₹3 crore. The same 12% in a ₹4.5 crore sale pays ₹54 lakh. Two things quietly reduce it in real deals: an ESOP pool created just before the sale, and liquidation preference, where investors take their money back before founders see anything. In a down-round sale, the preference can wipe a founder's payout to zero even though the equity percentage still looks healthy on paper.
when: An acquisition offer has arrived and you want your own number before you reply.
You are deciding whether to raise more or sell now, and need to know what each path pays.
You are an angel investor working out what your stake returns at a given exit.
mistakes: Reading the company's sale price as your payout. Only your equity percentage is yours.
Forgetting liquidation preference, which is paid to investors first and can leave founders with nothing in a modest sale.
Ignoring dilution between now and the exit - every future round shrinks the percentage you are using today.

fd.what: A fixed deposit pays a fixed rate for a fixed term, and the only decision that really changes the outcome is whether the interest is reinvested. 1,00,000 rupees at 7% for 5 years pays 35,000 in simple terms, but 40,255 if the interest compounds quarterly - and banks compound quarterly by default. The calculator shows both, plus the post-tax figure, because TDS on interest above 40,000 a year is what turns a 7% FD into about 4.9% for a taxpayer in the 30% slab.
fd.formula: Maturity = P x (1 + r / n)^(n x t), where r is the annual rate, n the compounds per year (4 for quarterly) and t the years. Interest = Maturity - P.
when: You are parking a lump sum and want the post-tax maturity, not the advertised rate.
You are comparing a bank FD with a small-finance bank FD that pays 0.5-1% more.
You are deciding between a 3-year and a 5-year FD and want the rupee difference.
mistakes: Comparing an FD rate against an equity fund's return. The FD is contractual; the fund is not.
Ignoring TDS. For anyone in the 30% slab, an FD's real return is roughly the rate minus 30%.
Breaking an FD early without checking the penalty - typically 0.5-1% of the rate.

franchise.what: A franchise or store ROI calculator answers the one question that decides whether to open: how long until I get my money back? The upfront cost of a store - franchise fee, deposit, fit-out, initial stock - is large and mostly sunk, and the monthly profit is what pays it back. An outlet that costs ₹25 lakh to open and makes ₹1.5 lakh a month takes about 17 months to pay back, and that is the number to compare against the franchise agreement's term.
franchise.formula: Payback Period in months = Starting Investment ÷ Monthly Profit. A ₹25 lakh investment earning ₹1,50,000 a month pays back in about 17 months. Return on investment is the yearly profit divided by the investment: ₹18,00,000 ÷ ₹25,00,000 = 72% a year, which looks excellent until you check whether the ₹1.5 lakh is the realistic month or the best month. Payback past the agreement's term means the model does not work.
when: You are evaluating a franchise offer and want the payback before signing.
You are comparing two locations with different rents and expected sales.
You are deciding whether to open a second outlet.
mistakes: Using the franchisor's projected sales instead of a conservative figure of your own.
Leaving working capital out of the investment. The store needs stock and cash before it earns.
Ignoring the royalty and marketing fees, which come off monthly profit before you see it.

freelance.what: A freelancer hourly rate calculator works out what you must charge per hour to reach your target income - and the answer is always higher than freelancers first guess. The reason is that a freelancer's billable hours are a fraction of the hours worked. Sales, invoicing, learning, admin and gaps between projects are all real time that nobody pays for, and a rate set on a 40-hour week is a rate that will leave you underpaid.
freelance.formula: Hourly Rate = Target Monthly Income ÷ Billable Hours per Month. If you want ₹1,00,000 a month, work 40 hours a week but only 50% of them are billable, and you work 4 weeks, that is 80 billable hours. ₹1,00,000 ÷ 80 = ₹1,250 an hour. Charge ₹800 and you will earn ₹64,000, no matter how hard you work. The billable percentage is the number freelancers consistently overestimate.
when: You are quoting a client and want a rate that actually pays you.
You are moving from a job to freelancing and want to match your old salary.
You are deciding whether a project at a given price is worth taking.
mistakes: Assuming every working hour is billable. Most freelancers bill 50% to 70% of their time at best.
Setting the rate from a competitor's price instead of from the income you need.
Forgetting tax, and the fact that you pay your own PF, insurance and holidays.

funnel.what: A marketing funnel calculator shows what you pay at every step - per click, per lead and per sale - so you can see exactly where the money is leaking. Each stage has its own cost, and each stage's cost is the previous one divided by its conversion rate. Most businesses know their ad spend and their sales and nothing in between, which makes it impossible to tell whether the problem is the ad, the landing page or the sales follow-up.
funnel.formula: CPC = Ad Spend ÷ Clicks. CPL = Ad Spend ÷ Leads. CPA = Ad Spend ÷ Conversions. Spend ₹50,000 for 2,500 clicks, 250 leads and 25 sales: CPC is ₹20, CPL is ₹200 and CPA is ₹2,000. Now you can see that doubling the lead-to-sale rate to 20% halves the CPA to ₹1,000, which is far cheaper than trying to halve the CPC.
when: A campaign is not profitable and you want to find which stage is failing.
You are setting targets for CPC, CPL and CPA before launching.
You are comparing two channels that look similar on ad spend alone.
mistakes: Optimising CPC when the leak is further down the funnel. Cheap clicks that never convert are worthless.
Measuring a channel on its last click when the customer saw three touchpoints first.
Comparing CPA across channels without checking the quality of the customers each one brings.

gratuity.what: Gratuity is the lump sum an employer pays when you leave a job after five years or more of continuous service. It is built on your last drawn basic salary plus dearness allowance, not on your full monthly CTC, and that is the single fact most people get wrong when they estimate it. This calculator works out the statutory figure under the Payment of Gratuity Act from the salary and completed years you enter, so the number is in front of you before an offer letter or a settlement does it for you.
gratuity.formula: Gratuity = last drawn basic + DA, multiplied by 15, divided by 26, multiplied by completed years. The 15/26 is the statutory rate: fifteen days of salary for each completed year, where a month is treated as 26 working days. So a basic plus DA of 50,000 with 10 completed years gives 50,000 x 15 / 26 x 10 = 2,88,461. Employers outside the Act use the same 15/26 in practice, but the salary base and the rounding of part-years can differ.
when: You are resigning or retiring and want the figure before HR sends the settlement.
You are comparing two offers and want to see what the gratuity is worth at the end of each.
You are checking a final settlement letter against the statutory formula.
mistakes: Using full CTC as the salary. Gratuity is built on basic plus DA only, so a CTC-based estimate comes out far too high.
Counting part-years as full years. Only completed years count, unless the fifth year carries 240 days or more of service.
Expecting gratuity before five years. Below five years of continuous service the statutory entitlement does not arise.

gross.what: Gross profit is what is left of your sales after you pay for the thing you sold, and gross margin is that number as a percentage. It is the first profit line and the most honest one, because nothing is hidden in it. A shop that sells a product for ₹1,000 that cost ₹600 has ₹400 of gross profit and a 40% gross margin. That ₹400 is not your profit yet - rent, salaries and marketing still have to come out of it - but if the 40% is not there in the first place, no amount of clever cost-cutting later will fix it. Gross margin tells you whether the business can work at all.
gross.formula: Gross Profit = Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold. Gross Margin % = (Gross Profit ÷ Revenue) × 100. Revenue of ₹10 lakh with COGS of ₹6 lakh gives ₹4 lakh of gross profit and a 40% margin. What counts as healthy depends on the business: physical products often run 40% to 60%, food 60% to 70%, and software 70% or more. A D2C brand selling at 25% gross margin is usually in trouble, because the ad spend alone can eat all of it.
when: You are pricing a product and want to see what margin the price actually leaves.
You are comparing two products and want to know which one is worth pushing.
You are preparing numbers for an investor and need the first profit line right.
mistakes: Calling gross profit your profit. Rent, salaries, marketing and tax still have to come out of it.
