Leaving delivery, packaging and payment gateway fees out of COGS. For a D2C brand those are a real part of what the sale costs.
Comparing your margin with a software company's. The same percentage means very different things in different businesses.

gst.what: A GST calculator does the two things you need constantly: adds GST to a price to get the final bill, and pulls GST out of an amount that already includes it. The second direction is the one that catches people, because a price quoted as inclusive of GST hides a smaller base than it looks. In India the rate is split into CGST and SGST for sales inside a state, or a single IGST for sales across states, but the total is the same.
gst.formula: GST Amount = Base Price × GST Rate ÷ 100, and the final price is Base + GST. A ₹1,000 base at 18% has ₹180 of GST and a ₹1,180 bill. Reverse it: if a bill is ₹1,180 inclusive of 18% GST, the base is 1,180 ÷ 1.18 = ₹1,000 and the tax is ₹180. The reverse direction uses division, not subtraction - subtracting 18% from ₹1,180 gives ₹967.60, which is wrong.
when: You are raising an invoice and need the GST amount and the total.
A price is quoted as inclusive and you need the base and the tax separated.
You are comparing a GST-inclusive price with a GST-exclusive one.
mistakes: Subtracting the GST rate from an inclusive price instead of dividing by (1 + rate). It always understates the base.
Forgetting that GST is charged on the discounted price when a discount is given before supply, but on the full price when it is given afterwards.
Treating GST collected as your money. It is held for the government and has to be paid.

gst_taxwealth.what: This GST calculator handles the slightly messier real-world case: a discount is applied first, then GST is charged on what remains, and the tax is split into CGST and SGST for you. The order matters. A 10% discount followed by 18% GST gives a different answer from 18% GST followed by a 10% discount on the gross, and getting it the wrong way round means your invoice does not match your books.
gst_taxwealth.formula: Discounted Base = Base Amount × (1 − Discount %). GST = Discounted Base × GST Rate. Total = Discounted Base + GST, with CGST and SGST each at half the rate for an intra-state sale. A ₹10,000 base with 10% discount and 18% GST: the base becomes ₹9,000, GST is ₹1,620 split as ₹810 CGST and ₹810 SGST, and the invoice total is ₹10,620.
when: You are issuing an invoice with a trade discount and GST on top.
You need the CGST and SGST split for an intra-state sale.
You are reverse-calculating the base from a GST-inclusive amount you were paid.
mistakes: Charging GST on the pre-discount amount. For a discount shown on the invoice, GST applies to the discounted value.
Splitting the tax evenly when the sale is inter-state - that should be IGST at the full rate, not CGST plus SGST.
Rounding CGST and SGST separately and letting the total drift by a rupee or two from the invoice.

homeemi.what: A home loan EMI calculator shows the fixed monthly payment on a housing loan and, just as importantly, what the loan costs you in total. An EMI has two parts - interest and principal - and in the early years almost all of it is interest. That is why a 20-year loan at 8.5% costs far more than the amount borrowed, and why a small prepayment in the first few years saves far more than the same amount paid later.
homeemi.formula: EMI = P × r × (1+r)^n ÷ ((1+r)^n − 1), where P is the loan amount, r the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100) and n the number of months. A ₹50 lakh loan at 8.5% for 20 years is an EMI of about ₹43,391, and the total paid over the term is about ₹1.04 crore - roughly double the loan. The same loan over 30 years drops the EMI to about ₹38,446 but raises the total cost to about ₹1.38 crore.
when: You are comparing loan offers from two banks at different rates and tenures.
You want to know how much a longer tenure costs you in total interest.
You are deciding whether to prepay or invest the extra money.
mistakes: Choosing the longest tenure for the lowest EMI. The monthly saving is small and the extra interest is large.
Ignoring that a floating rate means the EMI or the tenure can change, and the total is not fixed.
Forgetting processing fees, insurance and the stamp duty on the loan agreement, which are not in the EMI.

hra.what: An HRA exemption calculator works out how much of your house rent allowance escapes tax, and most salaried people claim less than they are entitled to. The exemption is the smallest of three amounts: the HRA you actually receive, the rent you pay minus 10% of basic salary, and 50% of basic salary if you live in a metro or 40% otherwise. Because it is the smallest of the three, the weakest link sets your exemption - so raising the rent you pay raises your exemption only up to a point.
hra.formula: Exemption = the least of: (1) HRA received, (2) Rent paid − 10% of basic salary, (3) 50% of basic salary in a metro or 40% elsewhere. If basic salary is ₹6 lakh, HRA is ₹3 lakh and rent is ₹2.4 lakh: option 2 is ₹2.4 lakh − ₹60,000 = ₹1.8 lakh, option 3 is ₹3 lakh in a metro, and the exemption is the smallest - ₹1.8 lakh. Note this works only in the old regime.
when: You pay rent and want to know how much exemption to claim before filing.
You are choosing between the old and new tax regime and want the HRA figure for the comparison.
You are negotiating a salary structure and want to see what HRA is worth to you.
mistakes: Claiming HRA in the new regime, where it is not available at all.
Assuming the full HRA is exempt. It is the smallest of three amounts, and rent minus 10% of basic is often the binding one.
Forgetting that paying rent to a family member is allowed only if the rent is actually paid and the landlord declares the income.

importduty.what: An import duty calculator works out what an imported consignment really costs by the time it clears customs, and the answer is always more than the invoice. Customs duty is charged first, and then IGST is charged on the value plus the duty, so the two compound instead of adding up neatly. A ₹1 lakh shipment at 20% duty and 18% IGST does not cost ₹1.38 lakh; it costs ₹1.42 lakh, because the IGST is calculated on ₹1.2 lakh and not on ₹1 lakh. On thin import margins that gap is the difference between a product that sells and one that does not.
importduty.formula: Customs Duty = Product Value × Duty Rate. IGST = (Product Value + Customs Duty) × IGST Rate. Landed cost = Product Value + Customs Duty + IGST. For ₹1,00,000 at 20% duty: duty is ₹20,000, IGST is 18% of ₹1,20,000 which is ₹21,600, and the landed cost is ₹1,41,600. Duty rates depend on the HSN code of the product, so always confirm the exact rate for your item before pricing it.
when: You are importing goods and want the true cost before you set a selling price.
You are comparing an imported product against a locally made one.
A shipment has landed and the customs bill is higher than you expected, and you want to see why.
mistakes: Charging IGST on the product value alone. It is charged on value plus duty, which is why the bill is always bigger than the simple sum.
Using a rough duty rate instead of the exact HSN code rate. The gap between two codes can be more than 10 percentage points.
Forgetting that customs duty is not the only charge - there can be a social welfare surcharge and clearance charges on top.

impval.what: An implied valuation is the value of a whole company worked backwards from one small deal. When someone says "50 lakh for 5%", they have just told you what they think the company is worth: 50 lakh is 5% of the company, so the company is worth 10 crore. Nobody wrote that number down - it is implied by the deal. That is the whole idea, and it is the fastest way to sanity-check any offer, because the person making it usually does not realise they have revealed their number.
impval.formula: Implied Valuation = Investment ÷ Equity % × 100. "50 lakh for 5%" is 50,00,000 ÷ 5 × 100 = ₹10 crore. Reversing it gives the implied equity: Investment ÷ Valuation × 100. The formula is the same one behind pre-money and post-money valuation - implied valuation is simply what you get when you run it backwards from the offer instead of forwards from the cap table.
when: Someone quotes a price and a stake together - "2 crore for 10%" - and you want the company value behind it.
You are comparing two offers on different stakes and need one number to compare them on.
An investor tells you your company is worth X and you want to test what that implies for the cheque they are offering.
mistakes: Treating the implied number as post-money when the investor meant pre-money. The difference is the cheque itself, and it is a real amount of equity.
Running the maths on a deal that includes a royalty or a loan - those are not equity, so the implied valuation is meaningless until the equity part is separated out.
Quoting an implied valuation as if a valuer certified it. It is a reading of an offer, not a registered valuation, and a CA or merchant banker is still needed for anything official.

incometax.what: An old vs new regime calculator tells you which of India's two income tax systems takes less from you this year, and the answer changes with almost every salary. The new regime gives lower slab rates but throws away most deductions. The old regime has higher rates but lets you subtract 80C, 80D, HRA and home loan interest before tax is worked out. So the comparison is not really about rates at all - it is about whether your deductions are large enough to beat the rate cut. Someone with no investments is almost always better off in the new regime; someone carrying a big home loan and full 80C is often better off in the old one.
incometax.formula: Old regime: tax on (Income − Deductions) using the old slabs. New regime: tax on Income using the new slabs, with almost no deductions. Whichever tax is lower wins. A plain ₹15 lakh salary with no investments is usually cheaper in the new regime, because there is nothing much to deduct. Add a ₹2 lakh home loan interest and a full ₹1.5 lakh of 80C, and the old regime can pull ahead again. Finding that crossover is what this calculator is for.
when: Your employer asks you to pick a regime at the start of the year and you do not want to guess.
You have just taken a home loan or started 80C investments and the answer may have changed.
You are comparing two job offers with different salary structures.
mistakes: Assuming the new regime is always better because the rates look lower. It is only better when your deductions are small.
Forgetting that the new regime still gives the standard deduction but not 80C, 80D or HRA.
Comparing last year's numbers with this year's slabs. Both regimes and their slabs have changed more than once in the last few years.

landed.what: Landed cost is the true total of getting a product into your warehouse, and it is almost always higher than the invoice. Manufacturing is only the first line - packaging, freight, insurance, customs clearance, and the last-mile delivery to your godown all land on the same unit. Founders who price from the manufacturing cost alone discover months later that they have been selling at a loss, because the number they used was never the real cost.
landed.formula: Landed Cost per Unit = (Manufacturing + Packaging + Shipping + Other Costs) ÷ Units. A batch of 1,000 units costing ₹4,00,000 to make, ₹40,000 to pack, ₹60,000 to ship and ₹30,000 in other charges lands at (4,00,000 + 40,000 + 60,000 + 30,000) ÷ 1,000 = ₹530 per unit. If you have been pricing at ₹500, every sale has been losing ₹30, and that is the whole point of calculating this.
when: You are setting a selling price and need the true cost of one unit.
You are comparing a domestic supplier with an imported one.
You are checking whether a product line is actually making money.
mistakes: Pricing from the manufacturing cost and leaving freight and clearance out.
Spreading one-off costs like tooling across a single batch instead of the volumes it will serve.
Forgetting that duties and taxes paid on import can be credited back later, so the cash cost and the real cost differ.

landunits.what: A land area unit converter turns square feet into the units Indian land is actually sold in - square yards, square metres, and the traditional units that still rule property deals in many states: guntha, cent, bigha and acre. This matters because a plot quoted in one unit and compared against another is not a fair comparison, and the traditional units differ from state to state, so a bigha in one state is not a bigha in the next.
landunits.formula: 1 square yard = 9 square feet. 1 square metre = 10.764 square feet. 1 acre = 43,560 square feet, which is 4,840 square yards. 1 guntha = 1,089 square feet, so 40 guntha make an acre. 1 cent = 435.6 square feet, so 100 cents make an acre. A 2,400 square feet plot is 266.7 square yards or about 223 square metres - useful when the buyer and the seller are quoting different units for the same land.
when: A plot is quoted in one unit and you need to compare it with another.
You are reading a sale deed or a 7/12 extract and need the area in a unit you understand.
You are converting between traditional units and square feet for a listing.
mistakes: Assuming a bigha or a guntha is the same everywhere in India. These units vary by state and sometimes by district.
Mixing up square feet and square yards, which differ by a factor of nine.
Converting the area but not checking the survey number and boundaries against the deed.

lovefun.what: A love calculator is a bit of fun - it takes two names, runs them through a letter-based formula and returns a compatibility percentage. It is not psychology, astrology or anything else with a claim behind it, and it should not be read as advice about a relationship. It exists because people enjoy it, and a calculator site should have a few tools that are just entertainment. Tank Metrics labels it as entertainment on purpose.
lovefun.formula: The score comes from counting how often the letters of the two names appear in the phrase 'loves', weighting the totals, and reducing the result to a percentage. There is no science in it - the same two names always give the same number, which is the only consistency it has. Treat the output as a party trick, not a prediction.
when: You want a light-hearted answer for a group chat.
You are curious what the same two names score more than once.
You want something quick and harmless to share.
mistakes: Taking the result seriously. It is entertainment and nothing more.
Reading anything into a low score. There is no basis for it.
Using it to make any decision about a real relationship.

ltv.what: Customer Lifetime Value is what one customer is worth to you across the whole relationship, not just the first sale. It takes the average order value, how often a customer buys in a year, how many years they stay, and your gross margin, and turns them into a single rupee figure. If a customer spends ₹1,000 four times a year for three years at a 50% margin, that customer is worth ₹6,000 of profit. LTV is the ceiling on what you can sensibly pay to win them - pay more and every new customer makes you poorer.
ltv.formula: LTV = Average Order Value × Purchases per Year × Customer Lifespan (years) × Gross Margin %. Margin matters: a customer who spends ₹12,000 but leaves you a 10% margin is worth ₹1,200, not ₹12,000. ₹1,000 × 4 × 3 × 50% = ₹6,000. The margin is what turns revenue into the profit that actually repays acquisition.
when: You are deciding how much you can afford to spend on ads per customer.
An investor asks for your unit economics and wants LTV next to CAC.
You are choosing between a high-margin niche and a high-volume one.
mistakes: Using revenue instead of profit - LTV must be built on gross margin or it overstates what a customer is worth.
Assuming customers stay for years because a few loyal ones do; the average lifespan is usually much shorter.
Counting only the first purchase and calling it lifetime value.

ltvcac.what: The LTV:CAC ratio puts the two unit-economics numbers side by side and answers the only question that matters for scaling: for every rupee spent winning a customer, how many rupees of profit come back? Divide lifetime value by acquisition cost. A ratio of 3:1 or better is the common rule of thumb - below 1:1 you lose money on every customer, and between 1 and 3 you are spending too much to grow. An LTV of ₹4,50,000 against a CAC of ₹1,80,000 is a ratio of 2.5:1, workable but not yet comfortable.
ltvcac.formula: LTV : CAC = Customer Lifetime Value ÷ Customer Acquisition Cost. Both sides must be measured over the same period and on the same basis - profit to profit. ₹4,50,000 of LTV over a ₹1,80,000 CAC gives 2.5 : 1. Below 1:1 the business loses money on every sale; 3:1 and above is the range investors look for.
when: You are preparing a fundraise and want the unit-economics slide right.
You are about to increase ad spend and want to know whether it still pays.
You are deciding whether to fix margin or fix acquisition cost first.
mistakes: Comparing revenue-based LTV to a fully-loaded CAC - the ratio then looks healthy while the business loses money.
Using a blended CAC that hides a channel where you lose money on every customer.
Treating 3:1 as a law; a low-margin business needs a higher ratio, a sticky one can live with less.

luckynumber.what: Your lucky number here is the single digit your full date of birth reduces to. Add every digit of the day, the month and the year — 15-06-1995 becomes 1+5+0+6+1+9+9+5 = 36 — then add the digits of that total, 3+6 = 9, and repeat until one digit from 1 to 9 is left. That final digit is what the tool calls your lucky number. It reads the same date the same way every time, so it is a fixed personal label rather than a daily draw, and it changes only if you were born on a different day.
luckynumber.formula: The tool strips the hyphens from the date of birth, adds all eight digits together, and if the total is more than nine it adds the digits of that total again. 1995-06-15 sums to 36, and 3+6 reduces to 9. The loop stops the moment a single digit 1-9 remains, which is why every date lands on one of nine numbers and none on a zero.
when: You are filling in a profile and want the number that matches your birth date.
A friend quotes their lucky number and you want to check which date it came from.
You are curious whether two people born the same day share a number.
mistakes: Adding the digits of the date exactly as written, hyphens and all, instead of the eight digits alone.
Stopping at a two-digit total like 36 instead of reducing it to 9.
Treating the number as a forecast. It is a fixed reduction of your date, not a prediction for the day.

marketplace.what: The Marketplace Fee Calculator shows what a seller actually banks from an order on Amazon, Flipkart or Meesho after the platform takes its cut. The commission is the headline charge, but it is rarely the only one: shipping, closing fees, payment-gateway charges and any fixed other fees come out of the same order. The tool subtracts all of them from the selling price and shows the amount that lands in your account. It is the number that decides whether a product is worth listing at a price the platform's own fee table can eat alive.
marketplace.formula: Total fees = selling price x commission rate / 100 + shipping fee + other fees. You receive = selling price minus total fees. Commission is charged on the selling price, not on your cost, so a 15% commission on a 1,000 rupee item is 150 rupees whether you made the product for 300 or for 800. Enter your real shipping and other fees, not a guess, or the answer flatters you.
when: You are pricing a product for a marketplace and want the net payout, not the gross price.
You are comparing the same product across two marketplaces with different fee tables.
A commission slab changed and you want to see how much of the price you just lost.
mistakes: Using the commission rate alone and forgetting shipping and closing fees, which can double the cut.
Assuming the fee applies to your cost. It applies to the selling price, so a thin-margin item can lose money.
Forgetting GST on the commission, which the platform charges on its own fee.

marketshare.what: The Market Share Calculator answers one question in plain numbers: out of everything sold in your market, how much is yours? Enter the total units sold in the market and the units you sold. That is it. You get your share as a percentage, plus how many units everyone else sold.
marketshare.formula: Your market share is your units divided by the total units, times 100. If 10,000 units were sold in the market and 6,000 of them were yours, your share is 6,000 / 10,000 = 60%. There is no compounding and no hidden step — it is one division. The tool also shows the other side: 4,000 units, or 40%, went to everyone else.
when: You want to know how big you are in your own market, not in revenue terms.
You are checking whether a claim like 'we are the market leader' is actually true.
You are setting a target and want a starting share to grow from.
mistakes: Mixing units with rupees. Count units against units, or money against money, never one of each.
Using a market figure that is bigger than the market you actually compete in, which flatters the share.
Reading a big share as automatically good — a 60% share of a tiny market is still a tiny business.
marketshare.intro: Suppose 10,000 units were sold in your market and 6,000 of them were yours. Here is your share.
marketshare.outro: 6,000 out of 10,000 is 60%. Change either number above and the share updates as you type — the arithmetic stays that simple.

markup.what: Markup and margin are two ways of describing the same profit, and mixing them up is one of the most expensive small mistakes in business. Markup is the profit as a percentage of your cost. Margin is the profit as a percentage of your selling price. So markup is always the bigger number on the same sale. A trader who thinks in markup but quotes a margin to a distributor can find themselves pricing 20% below what they intended.
markup.formula: Markup % = (Selling Price − Cost Price) ÷ Cost Price × 100. Margin % = (Selling Price − Cost Price) ÷ Selling Price × 100. Buy at ₹600, sell at ₹1,000: the profit is ₹400, which is a 66.7% markup but only a 40% margin. That gap is why a '40% margin' product is not a '40% markup' product, and confusing the two can cost you real money on a big order.
when: You are pricing a product and want to state the profit both ways correctly.
A buyer asks for a margin and you want to convert it into the price you must charge.
You are comparing your pricing with a competitor's and want a like-for-like number.
mistakes: Quoting markup as margin to a buyer, which makes your prices look higher than they are.
Working out a selling price by adding the margin to the cost, when a margin is a share of the selling price.
Forgetting that both numbers shrink the moment you offer a discount, because the selling price changed.

moicirr.what: MOIC and IRR are the two numbers a venture investor actually judges a deal on. MOIC is simple: how many times the money came back. Put in ₹1 and get ₹3, that is 3x. IRR is the same outcome expressed as a yearly rate, and it is the number that makes two deals comparable. A 3x in three years and a 3x in ten years are not the same achievement at all - the first is roughly 44% a year, the second about 12%. Founders who learn to speak in these two numbers stop being misunderstood by the people writing the cheques.
moicirr.formula: MOIC = Exit Amount ÷ Investment Amount. IRR is the annual rate at which the investment grows to the exit value over the years held: IRR = (Exit ÷ Investment)^(1 ÷ Years) − 1. ₹1 crore becoming ₹3 crore in 5 years is 3x MOIC and about 24.6% IRR. The same ₹3 crore in 10 years is still 3x MOIC but only about 11.6% IRR. Investors typically want 3x or more and 25% or better.
when: You are pitching and want to show the return your round offers, not just the valuation.
You are comparing two offers that return different amounts over different periods.
You are reporting to your own investors and need to state MOIC and IRR correctly.
mistakes: Quoting a multiple without the years. A 3x means nothing until you say over how long.
Comparing IRR across deals without noting that IRR assumes money is reinvested at the same rate, which is rarely true.
Using MOIC on a partial exit and treating it as the full picture - if only half the stake was sold, the multiple is only half-realised.

momyoy.what: Month-on-month compares this month with last month. Year-on-year compares this month with the same month a year ago. For almost every Indian business the YoY number is the honest one, because Diwali, the monsoon and the school calendar move demand so much that a MoM comparison mostly measures the festival, not the business. The calculator gives both, and the gap between them is the seasonality.
momyoy.formula: MoM % = (This Month - Last Month) / Last Month x 100. YoY % = (This Month - Same Month Last Year) / Same Month Last Year x 100.
when: A month looks bad and you want to know whether it is seasonality or a real decline.
You are presenting to an investor and need to show growth without the festive distortion.
You are setting next quarter's target and want a seasonal baseline to build on.
mistakes: Reporting MoM growth in a festive month as if it were a trend. October always beats September.
Comparing a 31-day month with a 28-day month without normalising for days.
Using YoY on a business that is less than a year old - there is nothing to compare against yet.

mrpreverse.what: An MRP reverse calculator starts from the printed price on the pack and works backwards to find what you as the manufacturer actually receive. This is the direction Indian founders need most, because the market sets the MRP long before you do - your competitor's ₹499 bottle is the price your product has to sit next to. From there you subtract the retailer's cut and the distributor's cut, and what is left is your landing price. If that number is below your cost, no amount of sales volume fixes it.
mrpreverse.formula: Landing Price = MRP × (1 − Retailer Margin %) × (1 − Distributor Margin %). An MRP of ₹500 with a 20% retailer margin and a 10% distributor margin gives ₹500 × 0.80 × 0.90 = ₹360 as your landing price. If your cost of goods is ₹300, your gross margin is ₹60, or 16.7%. If the cost is ₹380, you lose ₹20 on every unit sold, and the MRP is the thing that has to change.
when: You know the price your product must sell at and need to check the margin that leaves you.
A retailer asks for a deeper discount and you want to see what it costs you at the factory gate.
You are comparing two MRP points for the same product.
mistakes: Subtracting both margins from the MRP at once instead of one after the other - the second margin applies to a smaller number.
Forgetting GST, which sits outside the MRP in most cases and changes what you actually collect.
Assuming the margins are fixed. Retailers in different formats take very different cuts for the same product.

netmargin.what: The Net Profit Margin Calculator turns two figures — revenue and net profit — into the one percentage that says how much of every rupee of sales the business actually keeps. Net profit is the last line: after the cost of goods, after salaries and rent, after interest on any loan, and after tax. So this is the smallest and the most honest of the margin figures.
netmargin.formula: Net margin is net profit divided by revenue, multiplied by 100: `np` ÷ `rev` × 100. If a business earns ₹4,50,000 of revenue and keeps ₹1,80,000 after every cost and tax, the net margin is 1,80,000 ÷ 4,50,000 = 40%. Net profit is what remains after cost of goods, operating expenses, interest and tax; subtract any one of those later and the percentage rises.
when: You want to know how much of each rupee of sales the business keeps after everything is paid.
You are comparing your margin with others selling the same kind of product or service.
You are preparing accounts or a pitch and need the bottom-line percentage investors will ask for.
mistakes: Comparing the margin against a business in another industry. A grocery chain at 3% can be healthy while a software company at 3% is in trouble; the fair comparison is within the same trade.
Using profit before tax and calling it net. Net means after tax and after interest, which is why it is lower than the operating margin on the same revenue.
Reading a high percentage on a small revenue as a strong business. 40% of ₹4,50,000 is ₹1,80,000 — a large margin on a tiny turnover is still a small profit.
netmargin.intro: Take a business with ₹4,50,000 of revenue that keeps ₹1,80,000 after every cost and tax. Here is the net margin.
netmargin.outro: 40% is a strong net margin for most trades. If your figure is much lower, the leak is below the gross line — look at overheads, interest and tax before you look at price.

nps.what: NPS, the National Pension Scheme, is a retirement account the government runs through PFRDA. You put money in every year, it gets invested in equity and debt funds you choose, and you cannot touch it until 60. The return is not fixed - it depends on the funds. What the calculator does is project the corpus at 60 from your monthly contribution, your current age and an assumed return, so you can see whether the number you are saving today actually reaches the retirement you want.
nps.formula: Corpus = Monthly Contribution x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r] x (1 + r), where r is the monthly rate (annual / 12) and n is months to 60. On top of this, the employer's 14% of basic (under Section 80CCD(2)) and the extra 50,000 rupee deduction under 80CCD(1B) are added.
when: You are salaried and want to know how much the extra 50,000 rupee NPS deduction under 80CCD(1B) is actually worth.
You are choosing between NPS and PPF and want the projected corpus side by side.
You want to see what happens if you start 10 years later - the answer is usually brutal.
mistakes: Assuming the calculator's return is guaranteed. NPS equity funds swing; a 10% assumption is a planning number, not a promise.
Forgetting that 40% of the corpus must buy an annuity at 60. The lump sum you can withdraw is smaller than the corpus shown.
Comparing NPS with an ELSS fund on tax alone. NPS locks the money to 60; ELSS unlocks in three years.

numerology.what: The Numerology Calculator blends two inputs into one digit: the letters of your name and your date of birth. Each letter is turned into a number from its position in the alphabet — A is 1, J is 10, S is 19 — the values are added, the digits of the total are added again until a single digit is left, and the birth date is reduced the same way and folded in. The result depends on how the name is spelled, so 'Aarav' and 'Aarav ' can differ, and on the birth date underneath it.
numerology.formula: Take the name with everything except letters and digits removed. Add the character code of each remaining character, add the digits of the date of birth, then reduce the running total to one digit by summing its digits until a single 1-9 remains. Because a character code is used, an uppercase letter and a lowercase one do not give the same number.
when: You want the name-based number for a name-spelling or baby-name choice.
You have a name and a date and want one combined number, not two separate ones.
You are comparing how two spellings of the same name land differently.
mistakes: Expecting the same answer for 'Aarav' and 'aarav' — the tool reads character codes, so the case changes the result.
Leaving a middle name out and wondering why the number moved.
Reading the output as advice about the person rather than as a made-up number drawn from their own name.

numwords.what: Number to Words spells a figure out the Indian way - lakh and crore rather than million and billion. It is built for cheques, invoices, legal documents, rent agreements and any form that asks for the amount in words as well as in figures. Getting this wrong is a common reason a bank or a registrar sends a document back, so the tool shows the exact wording and the Indian grouping at once.
numwords.formula: The number is split from the left into crore, lakh, thousand and the final hundreds, because that is how the Indian system groups digits. Each group is then read as a number of up to three digits and joined with its scale word. Two and a half crore is 2,50,00,000, so the tool reads the groups rather than the individual digits.
when: You are filling in a cheque and need the amount in words.
You are drafting an invoice or an agreement that requires both forms.
You want to check that a figure written in words matches the digits.
mistakes: Mixing the Indian and international systems in one document.
Writing the words differently from the figures, which is the kind of mismatch a bank will query.
Dropping the 'only' at the end, which is the convention on cheques.
numwords.intro: Type a figure and the tool writes it the way an Indian cheque expects.
numwords.outro: Always check the words against the digits before you sign. A mismatch is what causes a payment to be held up.

opmargin.what:
Operating Margin answers whether the business makes money from trading, before the cost of the money it borrowed and the tax it owes. Revenue goes in, operating profit — what is left after the day-to-day costs of running the business — goes in, and the tool shows what share of each rupee of sales survives. It is the cleanest single read on whether the core operation works, because financing and one-off items stay out of it.

What matters is what “operating profit” leaves out. Interest on a loan is a cost of how the business is funded, not of what it sells; a tax charge depends on the whole company's position; a one-time asset sale is not trading. Strip those away and the margin shows the engine on its own. That is why it sits beside EBITDA rather than replacing it: EBITDA adds depreciation and amortisation back, so the two move together for an asset-light business and part ways for a factory.
opmargin.formula: Operating Margin = Operating Profit ÷ Revenue × 100. Revenue (rev) is the top line; Operating Profit (ebit) is what remains after the cost of goods sold and the operating expenses, but before interest and tax. ₹18,000 of operating profit on ₹45,000 of revenue is a 40% margin. Above 10% usually signals a healthy core; a negative margin means the operation itself is losing money and no amount of financing will fix it.
when: A busy month left little in the bank and you want to know whether the problem is the operation or the financing.
You are comparing your business with a competitor and want the one figure that ignores how each is funded.
You are preparing for a buyer or a lender and want to show the core business standing on its own.
mistakes: Putting net profit in the operating-profit field. Interest and tax are not operating costs, so using net profit understates the margin.
Comparing the margin across two companies without checking what each counts as operating. One may treat marketing as operating expense and another as a one-off.
Reading a single quarter as the trend. One-off costs and seasonality move the margin; trust the direction over several periods.

payback.what: CAC payback period is how many months of a customer's profit it takes to earn back what you spent winning them. It is the cash-flow version of the LTV:CAC ratio: a healthy ratio can still hide a payback so long that the business runs out of money before it profits. Enter the acquisition cost, the monthly revenue per customer and the gross margin, and you get the number of months. A payback under twelve months lets you reinvest quickly; three years means every new customer is a bet on money you will not see for a long time.
payback.formula: Payback Period (months) = CAC ÷ (Monthly Revenue per Customer × Gross Margin %). If a customer costs ₹5,000 to win, pays ₹1,000 a month and you keep 40% as margin, the payback is ₹5,000 ÷ ₹400 = 12.5 months. The margin is what makes the payback real; on revenue alone the same customer looks like a five-month payback that never arrives.
when: You are deciding how aggressively to spend on acquisition.
You have raised money and want to know how fast it recycles into new customers.
You are comparing two customer segments with very different payback speeds.
mistakes: Using revenue instead of gross-margin profit in the denominator, which halves the apparent payback.
Forgetting that a long payback is only survivable if the cash to fund it is already in the bank.
Ignoring churn - customers who leave before the payback month never repay the cost.

percent.what: A percentage calculator answers the single most common money question: what is X% of this number, and if the result is this, what percentage is that? Every discount, every tax rate, every growth figure and every margin is a percentage underneath, so this is the tool the rest of the site is built on. The trap is that percentages do not add up the way people expect - a 20% rise followed by a 20% fall does not leave you where you started, it leaves you 4% down.
percent.formula: Percentage of a number = Number × Percentage ÷ 100. A 15% discount on ₹2,400 is ₹360 off, so you pay ₹2,040. Reverse it: if ₹2,040 is what you paid after 15% off, the original is 2,040 ÷ 0.85 = ₹2,400. And the change between two numbers is (New − Old) ÷ Old × 100, which is how you check whether that 'huge' rise is actually big.
when: You are checking a discount or a tax amount on a bill.
You want to know by what percentage a number went up or down.
You are working out a margin or a share of a total.
mistakes: Adding and subtracting percentages as if they were plain numbers. They compound, and the order matters.
Calculating a rise from the new number instead of the old one. The base changes the answer.
Treating percentage points and per cent as the same thing. Going from 4% to 6% is a 2 percentage point rise but a 50% increase.

pitchscore.what: A Shark Tank pitch check runs your numbers against the questions the sharks actually ask, and tells you which ones are likely to get you grilled. On Shark Tank India the interrogation is remarkably consistent: what is your valuation and why, what are your revenue and margins, what does it cost to get a customer, and how many months of cash do you have left? A pitch that has clean answers to those four is a pitch that survives the room.
pitchscore.formula: There is no single formula - the check looks at ratios. Valuation against revenue shows how expensive the ask is. LTV against CAC shows whether growth is profitable; below 3 to 1 the sharks push back. Runway in months shows how much time the business has. Gross margin shows whether the product can fund its own growth. A ₹10 crore valuation on ₹1 crore of revenue is a 10x multiple, and the pitch has to justify it.
when: You are preparing a pitch and want to know your weak numbers first.
An investor has asked for your metrics and you want to sanity-check them.
You are deciding what to fix before you raise.
mistakes: Walking in with a valuation and no revenue to support it. The multiple is the first thing questioned.
Not knowing your CAC and LTV when asked, which reads as not knowing your own business.
Quoting a burn rate that implies a short runway without a plan for it.

ppf.what: A PPF calculator shows what your yearly Public Provident Fund contributions become over the 15-year lock-in, and the answer is more than most people expect because PPF compounds tax-free. You put in a fixed amount each year, the balance earns interest that is fully exempt, and the maturity amount is tax-free too - which makes it one of the very few EEE instruments in India. The cost is patience: the money is locked for 15 years, and that is the whole trade.
ppf.formula: The balance grows at the PPF rate compounded annually on each year's contribution, and the maturity value is the sum at the end of 15 years. ₹1.5 lakh a year at 7.1% for 15 years matures at roughly ₹40.7 lakh, of which about ₹22.5 lakh is your own contributions and the rest is tax-free interest. Contributing early in the financial year earns interest on that money for the whole year, so April beats March.
when: You are deciding between PPF and an equity SIP for a long-term goal.
You want to know what your current yearly contribution becomes at maturity.
You are using PPF for the 80C deduction and want to see the full picture, not just the tax saving.
mistakes: Depositing in March instead of April. You lose a full year's interest on that contribution.
Comparing the 7.1% PPF rate with an equity fund's long-run return without accounting for the fact that PPF's return is guaranteed and tax-free.
Forgetting the ₹1.5 lakh yearly cap, which cannot be exceeded in a single account.

prepost.what:
Pre-Money & Post-Money Valuation takes the term sheet as it is actually written — a price for the company before the cheque, and the cheque itself — and works out the two numbers that decide what a founder keeps. The pre-money is what the company was agreed to be worth with the new money still outside it; the post-money is that value plus the investment. The gap between them is not arithmetic decoration: it is the stake the new money buys.

The stake is the figure that gets argued about after the round closes. If the pre-money is ₹9 crore and the investor puts in ₹1 crore, the post-money is ₹10 crore and the cheque bought 10% — a tenth of the company, not a tenth of the old company. Founders who read only the pre-money assume the new investor's slice comes out of somewhere else, and are surprised when their own percentage is the one that falls. The tool shows both valuations and the equity given away on the same line so that surprise cannot happen.
prepost.formula: Post-Money Valuation = Pre-Money Valuation + Investment Amount. Equity Given = Investment Amount ÷ Post-Money Valuation × 100. Type the pre-money (pre) and the investment (amt); the tool adds them for the post-money, then divides the investment by that post-money figure to show the stake. A ₹9 crore pre-money plus a ₹1 crore cheque is a ₹10 crore post-money and 10% given away. The post-money, not the pre-money, is the base the stake is measured against.
when: A term sheet quotes a pre-money figure and you want the post-money and the stake it hands over.
You are deciding whether to raise at a lower pre-money for more money, and want to see how much more of the company that costs.
You are building a simple cap table and need the post-money before you can split it into stakes.
mistakes: Measuring the stake against the pre-money. 10% of the pre-money is not 10% of the company; the investment itself is part of the post-money base.
Reading the pre-money as the price of the whole company. It is the price before the new money, which is a smaller and less useful number on its own.
Adding the cheque to the pre-money but forgetting that the founder's own stake is diluted by exactly the equity given to the new investor.

propertyroi.what: A property ROI calculator answers the question every second-home buyer gets wrong: what did this flat actually earn me? There are two separate returns and they are easy to confuse. One is cash - the rent you collected. The other is on paper - how much the flat's value went up. A property can look like a great investment on appreciation alone and still have paid you almost nothing in cash, which matters on the day the tenant leaves or the EMI does not wait. This calculator shows both together, over the years you actually held it.
propertyroi.formula: Total gain = (Sale Value − Purchase Price) + Rent collected over the holding period. ROI = Total gain ÷ Purchase Price × 100, and the annualised figure spreads that over the years held. A flat bought at ₹60 lakh and sold at ₹85 lakh after 6 years with ₹1.2 lakh rent a year: the gain is ₹25 lakh plus ₹7.2 lakh, so ₹32.2 lakh on ₹60 lakh, about 54% in total and roughly 7.4% a year. Rental yield, which is just annual rent ÷ purchase price, is the number to compare against a fixed deposit.
when: You own a flat that is rented out and want to know the return you are actually earning.
You are deciding between a second property and a fixed deposit or a debt fund.
You are about to sell and want the full gain, cash plus appreciation, before you agree a price.
mistakes: Counting appreciation and ignoring the rent, or the other way round. The two together are the return.
Forgetting the money that went out - stamp duty, registration, brokerage, maintenance and the interest on the loan.
Comparing a 6% rental yield with a 7% fixed deposit without adding the appreciation, which is the whole reason people buy property.

propertyvalue.what: A property valuation is an estimate of what a flat, house or plot is worth today. For most homes the fastest honest way to get there is simple: the area you are buying, multiplied by the rate the locality is actually trading at per square foot. Banks, brokers and buyers all start from this number before they argue about anything else. The rate per square foot is the whole argument - a 1,000 sq ft flat is worth ₹80 lakh on one street and ₹1.6 crore two kilometres away, and the area never changed. So this calculator asks for the two numbers that matter and nothing else.
propertyvalue.formula: Property Value = Area (sq ft) × Price per Sq Ft. A 900 sq ft flat at ₹7,500 per sq ft is ₹67.5 lakh. A 1,400 sq ft flat at ₹11,000 per sq ft is ₹1.54 crore. The reverse is just as useful: if a broker quotes ₹1.2 crore for a 1,200 sq ft flat, the rate being asked is ₹10,000 per sq ft, and you can compare that against what nearby flats actually sold for. That single division is how you catch an overpriced listing.
when: You have seen a flat and want to sanity-check the asking price against the going rate per square foot.
You are comparing two localities and want both prices on the same per-square-foot basis.
A broker has quoted a lump sum and you want to see what rate per square foot it implies.
mistakes: Using the built-up area when the price is quoted on carpet area. The same flat can be 20% smaller on carpet area, and the rate per square foot then looks higher for no reason.
Taking the asking rate as the market rate. Asking prices sit above what actually closes, sometimes by 10% or more.
Ignoring the floor, the age of the building and the facing, which move the rate even within one building.

rashi.what: Rashi is the moon sign, and in Vedic astrology it is the sign that matters most - far more than the Western sun sign you probably already know. The moon moves through the twelve rashis in about two and a half days each, so two people born a week apart can sit in different rashis. This tool estimates the rashi from your birth date alone, which is the honest limit of a date-only calculation: the moon crosses a rashi boundary roughly every 54 hours, so a date near a boundary can fall either side. The page names the rashi in the traditional order, Mesha through Meena, and says plainly what the estimate can and cannot settle.
rashi.formula: The moon covers the whole zodiac in about 27.3 days, so it spends roughly 2.25 days in each rashi. This tool takes the day of the month from the date you enter, maps it in order onto the twelve rashis - Mesha, Vrishabha, Mithuna, Karka, Simha, Kanya, Tula, Vrishchika, Dhanu, Makara, Kumbha, Meena - and returns the one for that day. The day of the month stands in for the moon's position. A precise rashi needs the birth time, because the moon crosses a rashi boundary about every 54 hours and the crossing drifts through the month.
when: You want a quick moon sign and you remember only your birth date, not the time.
You are reading a panchang or a rashi forecast and want to know which rashi it is written for.
You are comparing your rashi with a friend's and neither of you has a birth record to hand.
mistakes: Treating the date-only rashi as final. Within a day of a boundary the real rashi needs your birth time.
Confusing rashi with the Western sun sign. They use the same twelve ideas in different languages and different dates.
Using a rashi estimate to time a muhurat, a wedding or a property purchase. Those need a full kundli from a jyotish.

rd.what: A recurring deposit is a monthly commitment to the same rate, with the bank paying interest on each instalment from the day it lands. 5,000 rupees a month for 5 years at 7% grows to about 3.6 lakh, of which 3 lakh is your own money. It is the deposit equivalent of a SIP, and the calculator's job is to show the interest separately from the contributions so the return is honest.
rd.formula: Maturity = sum of P x (1 + r / 4)^(quarters remaining), over each monthly instalment. Interest = Maturity - (P x months).
when: You want a fixed-return monthly habit and want to know the maturity before committing.
You are comparing an RD with a debt mutual fund for a 3-year goal.
You want to see what the last instalment earns versus the first - the difference surprises people.
mistakes: Expecting the advertised rate to apply to the whole balance. Each instalment earns only for the time it is in.
Missing an instalment and assuming no penalty. Banks charge it, and it can reset the rate.
Using an RD for a 10-year goal. Compounding equity usually wins over that horizon.

rentalyield.what: Rental Yield Calculator turns the rent a property earns into an annual percentage of what it cost. Multiply the monthly rent by twelve to get the yearly rent, divide that by the purchase price and multiply by 100. A home bought for 50,00,000 that rents for 20,000 a month earns 2,40,000 a year, which is a gross yield of 4.8%. The percentage is the point: it puts two properties of different prices on one scale, and it lets you compare property with a fixed deposit or a bond on the same footing.
rentalyield.formula: Annual rent = monthly rent x 12. Gross rental yield = annual rent / property price x 100. The tool uses the purchase price as the base, so the yield falls as the price rises even if the rent holds. This is a gross yield: it does not subtract maintenance, property tax, or the weeks the flat sits empty, so the true net yield is always lower.
when: You are comparing two flats at different prices and want a common yardstick.
You are checking whether a rental beats a fixed deposit on the same money.
You want to see how a small drop in rent moves the yield.
mistakes: Reading the gross yield as the return you keep — maintenance and vacancy come out of it first.
Dividing the rent by the loan amount instead of the property price.
Comparing a yield on a fully furnished flat with one on a bare shell without adjusting the price.

rentbuy.what: Rent vs Buy weighs the rent you would pay over a set number of years against what buying the same home costs before any loan. The rent side is the monthly rent multiplied by twelve and then by the years you are comparing. The buy side is the home price plus the one-time upfront costs — stamp duty, registration, brokerage, the moving-in expenses that never come back. The tool does not model a home loan, so it answers the narrower question of which side is smaller when you are paying cash or setting the loan aside for the moment.
rentbuy.formula: Total rent = monthly rent x 12 x years compared. Buy cost before loan = home price + upfront buy costs. The tool shows both and names the smaller one as the lower cost. It deliberately leaves out the EMI and the interest, so the buy figure is the cash you commit on day one and not the total you pay over the holding period.
when: You are renting and want to see the break-even against buying with cash.
You want the one-time cost of a purchase, separate from the loan.
You are explaining to someone why a lower rent can still lose over five years.
mistakes: Reading the buy figure as the full cost of owning — the loan interest is not in it.
Comparing a five-year rent total with a buy price for a home you would hold for twenty years.
Forgetting that stamp duty and registration sit inside the upfront number, not in the price.

retention.what: Retention is the share of customers who come back; churn is the share who leave. Together they decide whether growth compounds or leaks. If you start a month with 1,000 customers, end with 1,000 and added 100 new ones along the way, then 100 old customers left - retention is 90% and churn is 10%. A business can add customers every month and still shrink if churn is higher than acquisition. This calculator shows both, so the leak is visible before it empties the bucket.
retention.formula: Retention % = (Customers at End − New Customers) ÷ Customers at Start × 100; Churn % = 100 − Retention %. Start with 1,000, end with 1,000, add 100 new: retained = 1,000 − 100 = 900, so retention is 90% and churn 10%. The subtraction is what most founders miss - new customers mask old ones leaving, and only the calculation shows the truth.
when: You are measuring whether a subscription or repeat-purchase business is healthy.
You are deciding how much to invest in retention versus acquisition.
You want to see how a churn change affects growth over a year.
mistakes: Counting new customers as retention, which hides the ones who left.
Measuring churn monthly but judging the business on annual numbers, or the reverse.
Assuming a small churn is harmless - 5% a month is more than half the base gone in a year.

revmul.what: The Revenue Multiple divides what a company is being valued at by its yearly revenue. If a business earns ₹1 crore a year and someone offers ₹5 crore for it, the multiple is 5x. It is the quickest sanity check in a valuation because revenue is the hardest number to argue about: it is on the invoices, not on an assumption sheet. It says nothing about profit, so it is only meaningful next to a margin figure.
revmul.formula: Revenue Multiple = Valuation ÷ Annual Revenue. The tool takes the valuation you enter and divides it by the yearly revenue, then shows the answer as a number of times. A 3x multiple means the buyer is paying three rupees for every one rupee of yearly sales. Change either figure and the multiple moves, which is the point: the same ₹5 crore price is cheap at 2x and expensive at 12x.
when: A founder has an offer or a term sheet and wants to know whether the price is in a normal range.
You are comparing two companies in the same line of business and revenue is the only figure you have for both.
You are setting your own asking price and want to work backwards from a multiple buyers in your category actually pay.
mistakes: Using the wrong revenue. A buyer means the last twelve months, or the next twelve, and the two can differ by 40% in a growing business — the multiple swings with it.
Reading a high multiple as good news. A 10x revenue price on a business with 5% margins is worse than a 3x price on one with 30% margins.
Mixing recurring and one-off revenue. Subscription revenue earns a far higher multiple than project revenue, so a blended figure misleads both sides.

roas.what: Return on Ad Spend tells you how many rupees of revenue came back for every rupee spent on ads. Divide revenue from ads by the ad spend: ₹1,00,000 of revenue from ₹20,000 of ads is a ROAS of 5x. It is the fastest read on whether a campaign is working, but revenue is not profit. A 5x ROAS on a product with a thin margin can still lose money once cost of goods, shipping and returns are paid. Use ROAS to screen campaigns, then check the margin before scaling.
roas.formula: ROAS = Revenue from Ads ÷ Ad Spend. ₹1,00,000 ÷ ₹20,000 = 5x. To turn it into a break-even test, divide 1 by your gross margin: at a 25% margin you need a ROAS above 4x just to cover the cost of the product, before any profit. A high ROAS on a low-margin product can still be a loss.
when: You are checking whether a campaign is worth scaling.
You are comparing channels with different costs and returns.
You are setting a target ROAS for an agency or a media buyer.
mistakes: Treating revenue-based ROAS as profit - it ignores cost of goods, shipping and returns.
Comparing ROAS across products with different margins as if the number were comparable.
Scaling on a good ROAS without checking that the extra orders can actually be fulfilled.

roce.what:
Return on Capital Employed answers a question ROI cannot: how hard is every rupee inside this business working, whether it came from you or from a lender? Capital employed is shareholders' equity plus long-term debt, so ROCE puts a debt-free shop and a heavily borrowed one on the same ruler. Two businesses can post the same ROI and very different ROCE, and the gap is almost always the borrowing.

Reach for it when you are weighing an acquisition, a new machine or a second outlet against the money already tied up in the first one. It is a before-interest number: the tool divides operating profit by capital employed and stops there, because how the capital was financed is exactly the thing you are trying to see past.
roce.formula: ROCE is operating profit (EBIT) divided by capital employed, times 100. In this tool 'Operating Profit' is the ebit field and 'Capital Employed' is the ce field. Capital employed is total assets minus current liabilities, which is the same as shareholders' equity plus long-term debt. Rs 4,50,000 of operating profit on Rs 18,00,000 of capital employed gives 25%. Because the numerator is struck before interest and tax, ROCE does not move when the debt does, and that is what makes two differently financed companies comparable.
when: You are comparing two companies with different debt levels and want a like-for-like return.
You are deciding whether a new machine or outlet earns more than the capital already sitting in the business.
An investor asks how well the company uses the whole balance sheet, not just the founders' money.
mistakes: Putting profit after interest in the numerator. ROCE takes EBIT on purpose so the debt neither flatters nor punishes the number; net profit belongs in ROE, not here.
Tinkering with capital employed - subtracting short-term creditors twice, or dropping cash entirely - so the ratio jumps while nothing real has changed.
Cheering a high ROCE on a business with almost no capital employed. A services firm that rents everything can show 200% and still own nothing worth buying.

roi.what:
Return on Investment is the bluntest of the return measures: what did I get back compared with what I put in? The tool takes net profit - after every cost, including interest and tax - and divides it by the investment cost. Rs 1,00,000 of profit on Rs 10,00,000 spent is 10%. Nothing here is annualised and nothing is adjusted for risk, so two projects showing the same ROI are only comparable if they took the same time to pay back.

Use it as the first filter on any spend that has a number attached: an ad campaign, a machine, a course, a shop fit-out. It is deliberately simple, and that simplicity is the weakness - it will not tell you whether the 10% took six months or six years. Bring in payback or CAGR when the timing is what you are actually deciding.
roi.formula: ROI is net profit divided by investment cost, times 100. Here 'Net Profit' is the profit field and 'Investment Cost' is the inv field. Net profit is what survives goods, salaries, ads, fees, interest and tax - not revenue, and not gross margin. Rs 10,00,000 put in for Rs 1,00,000 of net profit is a 10% ROI. The tool does not divide by the number of years, so a 10% ROI over one year and a 10% ROI over five years read identically on this page.
when: You are judging one ad campaign, machine or course before you release the money.
You want a single number to rank several small spends that all take about the same time.
Someone quotes an ROI figure and you want to reproduce it from their profit and their cost.
mistakes: Feeding gross profit or revenue into the numerator, which turns a 10% ROI into something that reads like 40%.
Leaving out the costs that arrive after the sale - GST, marketplace commission, returns, gateway fees - so the profit is the optimistic version.
Treating a 10% ROI over six months as equal to a 10% ROI over five years; the tool does not annualise, so you have to.

royalty.what: In a royalty deal an investor takes a fixed percentage of your revenue every month instead of, or in addition to, equity, until a set amount is repaid. It is popular with sharks because it returns cash quickly, and with founders because it costs far less ownership. Enter the investment, the royalty rate and expected annual revenue, and the calculator shows the yearly royalty and how many years it takes to repay. A royalty is cheap in equity but expensive in cash flow - it is charged on sales, whether or not you made a profit.
royalty.formula: Annual Royalty = Expected Annual Revenue × Royalty Rate %; Payback Period (years) = Investment ÷ Annual Royalty. On ₹1.8 crore of revenue at an 18% royalty the investor takes ₹32.4 lakh a year, repaying a ₹4.5 crore investment in about 14 years. Higher sales repay faster; a slow year stretches the payback while the royalty still has to be paid.
when: A shark offers royalty instead of a large equity stake.
You want to keep ownership and are willing to pay from monthly revenue.
You are comparing royalty-heavy against equity-heavy offers.
mistakes: Judging the deal on ownership alone and ignoring the monthly cash it takes out.
Assuming revenue will always grow, which shortens the payback on paper only.
Forgetting that royalty is paid on sales even in a loss-making month.

runrate.what: A run rate takes your most recent month and asks what a full year would look like if every month were the same. It is the fastest way to describe a business that is growing quickly, and the easiest way to fool yourself. A ₹25 lakh month gives a ₹3 crore run rate, which sounds like a serious business - until you notice that month included a festive spike that will not repeat. Run rate is a useful direction-of-travel number and a poor promise, and investors know the difference.
runrate.formula: Annual Run Rate = Last Month's Revenue × 12. ₹25 lakh a month gives ₹3 crore a year. For a business with a strong seasonal peak, a three-month average is more honest: ₹25 lakh, ₹18 lakh and ₹20 lakh average ₹21 lakh, so the run rate is ₹2.52 crore rather than ₹3 crore. Use the monthly figure when you are growing steadily and the average when you are not.
when: You are raising money and want to state the current size of the business.
You are tracking your own growth month on month and want a yearly view.
You are comparing your run rate against a target you set at the start of the year.
mistakes: Presenting a festive-month run rate as if it were the annual figure. Anyone who looks at the monthly trend will see it.
Using run rate for a business with lumpy, contract-based revenue. It flatters a business with one big order in the month.
Confusing revenue run rate with profit run rate. A ₹3 crore revenue run rate can sit on a loss.

saas.what: ARPU, MRR and ARR are the three numbers every subscription or app business is judged on. MRR is the recurring revenue you can expect every month, ARR is the same annualised, and ARPU is the average revenue per user. Investors look at these before almost anything else, because recurring revenue is far more valuable than one-off sales - it can be forecast, and it compounds as customers stay.
saas.formula: MRR = Total Monthly Revenue from subscriptions. ARR = MRR × 12. ARPU = MRR ÷ Active Users. ₹8,00,000 of monthly subscription revenue is ₹96,00,000 ARR. With 2,000 active users the ARPU is ₹400 a month. Two things move these numbers: new customers raise MRR, and churn lowers it. A business growing MRR while losing 8% of customers a month is filling a leaking bucket.
when: You are raising money and need to state MRR and ARR correctly.
You are comparing two pricing plans and want to see which raises ARPU.
You are tracking whether growth is real or just offsetting churn.
mistakes: Counting one-off setup fees or annual prepayments as MRR. Only recurring revenue belongs in it.
Reporting ARR from a single good month instead of the current run rate.
Watching ARPU without watching churn. Higher ARPU with high churn still shrinks the business.

savegoal.what: The Savings Goal Planner tells you how much to put aside each month to reach a target, or how long a monthly amount will take to get there. It is for a down payment, an emergency fund, a wedding or any goal with a number and a date attached.
savegoal.formula: The tool works from the target, what you already have, and what you can save each month. If you fix the monthly amount, it solves for the time; if you fix the time, it solves for the monthly amount. Where a return is included, the existing balance and each monthly contribution both earn it, which is why the total you contribute is less than the goal.
when: You have a target amount and a date and want to know the monthly number.
You are deciding whether to save more or push the date out.
You want to see how much of the goal your savings are doing versus the returns.
mistakes: Ignoring inflation. A goal ten years away costs more than the same goal today.
Counting on a return that is not guaranteed, especially over a short period.
Saving whatever is left at the end of the month instead of a fixed amount on payday.
savegoal.intro: Say you want ₹5,00,000, you already have ₹1,00,000, and you can put aside ₹15,000 a month.
savegoal.outro: Change the monthly amount above and the time to the goal moves with it. Even a small increase, held for years, moves the date a long way.

simpledisc.what: The Discount Calculator works out what a percentage off actually takes off a price. Enter the original price and the discount, and it shows two things: the rupees you save and the price you finally pay. That is the number that decides whether a sale is worth acting on — not the percentage, which is the part shops advertise because it sounds bigger than it is.
simpledisc.formula: The saving is the original price multiplied by the discount, divided by 100: `price` × `disc` ÷ 100. The final price is the original minus that saving: `price` − saving. At ₹2,000 with a 25% discount the saving is ₹500 and the final price is ₹1,500. Two discounts applied one after another are not added together — 30% then 20% leaves you paying 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the price, which is 44% off, not 50%.
when: A marketplace or shop shows a flat percentage off and you want the rupee amount before you decide.
You are comparing two sale prices where the discounts and the original prices are both different.
A coupon stacks on top of an existing sale and you want to know the real final price.
mistakes: Adding two discounts together. A 30% discount followed by a 20% one is 44% off the original, not 50%, because the second discount applies to the already-reduced price.
Reading the discount as a share of the final price. The percentage is taken off the original marked price; once the price has dropped, the same rupees are a larger percentage of what is left.
Comparing discount percentages across different prices. 40% off ₹2,000 saves ₹800, which is more than 50% off ₹1,000 at ₹500.
simpledisc.intro: Take a ₹2,000 jacket with 25% off in a sale. Here is what the discount takes off.
simpledisc.outro: The percentage is the shop's number; the ₹500 saving and the ₹1,500 final price are yours. Change either figure above and both move together.

simpleint.what: Simple interest is charged only on the original amount, never on the interest already earned. 1,00,000 rupees at 10% for 3 years earns 30,000 - flat, every year, on the same 1,00,000. Compound interest on the same terms earns 33,100. The 3,100 rupee gap is small over three years and enormous over thirty, which is why knowing which one applies matters more than the rate itself.
simpleint.formula: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time / 100. Total = Principal + Interest. For a part-year, Time is months / 12.
when: A lender quotes a flat rate and you want the simple-interest figure to compare against a reducing-balance loan.
You are lending to a friend or relative and want a clear number in rupees.
You are checking a fixed-deposit or a bond coupon that pays simple interest.
mistakes: Treating a flat rate as the real cost of a loan. A flat 10% on a reducing balance is closer to 18%.
Mixing up simple and compound when the period is long. Over 10 years the difference is not small.
Forgetting TDS on interest above the threshold, which reduces what you actually receive.

sip.what: A SIP is a fixed amount invested in a mutual fund every month. The point of the calculator is compounding: 10,000 rupees a month for 20 years at 12% is not 24 lakh of contributions, it is about 99 lakh, and almost three quarters of that is growth you never deposited. The calculator separates your contribution from the growth, which is the number that makes people start a SIP rather than think about it.
sip.formula: Future Value = P x [((1 + i)^n - 1) / i] x (1 + i), where P is the monthly amount, i is the monthly rate (annual / 12 / 100) and n is the number of instalments. Contribution = P x n; Growth = Future Value - Contribution.
when: You are deciding whether to increase a SIP by 5,000 rupees a month and want to see the 20-year difference.
You want to know how many years a goal needs, given what you can afford monthly.
You are choosing between a 10% and a 12% fund and want to see whether the gap is worth the risk.
mistakes: Using the fund's last-year return as the assumption. SIPs are planned on a long-run average, not last year's best.
Stopping the SIP in a falling market, which is exactly when you buy the most units per rupee.
Ignoring the expense ratio. A 1% higher ratio costs roughly a tenth of a 20-year corpus.

split.what:
Bill Splitter divides one shared amount by the number of people paying it, and nothing else. It is the tool for the last two minutes at a table: the total is on the bill, four of you are paying, each owes a quarter. The arithmetic is a single division, so the value is not in the maths - it is in having the per-head figure before anyone starts rounding in their head and the numbers stop agreeing.

It handles the plain case on purpose. It does not decide who ordered the paneer, it does not add a tip, and it does not re-split a bill that already carries a service charge. That is a feature: an equal split is the only split that ends an argument, and every uneven arrangement is easier to settle once the equal share is on the table.
split.formula: Each person pays the total bill divided by the number of people. In this tool 'Total Bill' is the total field and 'Number of People' is the people field. Rs 1,000 across 4 people is Rs 250 each. When the total does not divide evenly - Rs 1,000 across 3 - the tool shows Rs 333.33, and the honest fix is for one person to absorb the odd paise or for everyone to round up and leave the difference in the tip.
when: A group dinner or a trip ends and the bill has to be settled on the spot.
Roommates split a shared utility or grocery bill evenly each month.
Co-founders or a small team split a shared subscription or a taxi fare.
mistakes: Splitting the pre-tax subtotal and forgetting the GST and service charge already printed on the bill.
Dividing by the number of people who came rather than the number who are paying, when someone is being treated.
Rounding every share down and leaving the last person with the shortfall; round up, or let one person take the odd rupees.

stampduty.what: A stamp duty calculator works out the money you pay the government on the day you register a property, and it is almost always more than a buyer has budgeted. Stamp duty is a state tax on the transaction and registration is the fee to record it in your name; together they add roughly 6% to 8% of the property value in most states, and in a few they cross 10%. On a ₹80 lakh flat that is ₹5 lakh to ₹8 lakh, paid in one go, and it cannot be added to the loan. This calculator shows the two charges and the total you have to carry to the sub-registrar's office.
stampduty.formula: Stamp Duty = Property Value × Stamp Duty Rate, and Registration = Property Value × Registration Rate. Total cost of buying = Property Value + Stamp Duty + Registration. A ₹80 lakh flat in a state charging 6% stamp duty and 1% registration costs ₹80 lakh + ₹4.8 lakh + ₹80,000, so ₹85.6 lakh on the day. Some states charge stamp duty on the higher of the agreement value and the circle rate, so the government's own floor price can push the bill up.
when: You are about to register a property and want the exact cash you must arrange on that day.
You are comparing two states or two cities and the transaction cost changes your budget.
You are working out the true all-in cost of a purchase, not just the price the seller quoted.
mistakes: Budgeting for the price and forgetting the duty, which on a ₹80 lakh flat is several lakh more.
Assuming stamp duty is the same everywhere. It is a state subject and varies by state, by buyer (women sometimes pay less) and by property type.
Forgetting that stamp duty cannot be financed in the home loan, so it has to be your own cash.

takehome.what: Take-home is what lands in your bank after the employer deducts TDS, the employee's PF share, and professional tax. The gap between CTC and take-home is bigger than most people expect - on a 12 lakh CTC, the monthly credit is often closer to 80,000 rupees than 1,00,000, because the employer's PF and gratuity provisions are inside the CTC number but never reach you. The calculator does that subtraction line by line so the offer letter is readable.
takehome.formula: Take-home = Gross Salary - Employee PF (12% of basic) - Professional Tax - TDS. Gross = CTC - Employer PF - Gratuity - other retirals. TDS is then computed on the taxable gross after the standard deduction of 75,000 rupees.
when: You have an offer letter in front of you and want to compare two CTCs on what you actually get monthly.
You are negotiating and need to know what a 1 lakh CTC increase is worth in hand.
You want to check whether the old or the new tax regime leaves you more this year.
mistakes: Comparing a CTC that includes a big variable bonus against one that does not. The bonus is not monthly cash.
Forgetting that employer PF sits inside CTC. It is your money, but it is not in your account this month.
Assuming the TDS the employer deducts is the final tax. It is an estimate, and the March true-up is real.

tam.what: TAM / SAM / SOM sizes a market before you commit money to it. TAM is everyone who could ever buy this kind of product. SAM is the slice you can actually reach — the cities you ship to, the customers your price suits. SOM is the slice you can realistically win in the next few years with the team and budget you have. Investors ask for all three because a huge TAM with a tiny SOM tells them the market exists but you have no route into it.
tam.formula: SAM is TAM times the share of it you can serve, as a percentage. SOM is SAM times the share of that you expect to win, also as a percentage. The tool multiplies through and shows both. The important part is the assumption behind each percentage: if you claim 40% of a reachable market, you are claiming to be the biggest player in it, which needs a reason.
when: You are writing the market slide for a pitch and want numbers that survive a question.
You are deciding which customer segment to build for first.
You want to check whether the market you are aiming at is big enough to matter.
mistakes: Quoting the whole TAM as your opportunity. It is the least useful of the three numbers on its own.
Claiming a SOM that would make you the market leader without a plan to get there.
Sizing the market in rupees when your customers buy in units, which hides how few buyers there are.
tam.intro: Take a market you could sell into. Here is how the three layers stack up.
tam.outro: The SOM is the number to defend. Anyone can claim a large TAM; the SOM is where you say how you actually get in.

tip.what: The Tip Calculator works out how much to leave and what the bill comes to once it is added. Give it the bill and a percentage, and it returns the tip amount and the total you hand over. That total is the figure that matters when you are paying cash, splitting with friends, or checking a bill against what you expected.
tip.formula: The tip amount is the bill multiplied by the tip percentage, divided by 100: `bill` × `tip` ÷ 100. The total is the bill plus the tip amount: `bill` + tip amount. On a ₹1,000 bill at 10%, the tip is ₹100 and you pay ₹1,100. If you want to tip on the pre-tax bill, enter the pre-tax figure — the percentage is applied to whatever number is in the bill field.
when: You are at a restaurant and want to leave a fair, round amount without doing the arithmetic in your head.
The bill already carries a service charge and you want to see what an extra tip would add.
You are splitting a bill and need each person's share of the bill plus tip.
mistakes: Tipping on the total instead of the bill. If the number you enter already includes the tip, applying the percentage again charges it twice.
Leaving a second tip when a service charge is already printed. The service charge is the tip; check the bill before you add more.
Splitting the bill and then tipping on each share. Work out the tip on the whole bill once, then divide the total, or the rounding on each share inflates it.
tip.intro: Take a ₹1,000 bill and a 10% tip. Here is what you leave and what you pay.
tip.outro: The tip is ₹100 on a ₹1,000 bill, so the total is ₹1,100. Change the bill or the percentage above and both the tip and the total follow.

utilization.what: Utilization rate is the share of your team's paid hours that actually goes to billable client work, and for an agency it is the number the whole payroll hangs on. If you bill 1,200 hours against the 1,600 hours your team was paid to be available, utilization is 75%, and the other 25% - internal meetings, admin, pitching, training - is real cost you carry but can never invoice. This calculator divides billable hours by the available hours you paid for and returns that percentage, so you can see how much of the payroll is actually earning.
utilization.formula: Utilization rate = billable hours / available hours x 100. Available hours is what you paid the team for: number of people x hours per week x weeks in the period. Bill 1,200 hours out of 1,600 available and the rate is 1,200 / 1,600 x 100 = 75%. The tool returns that percentage and nothing else. Track it per person and per month rather than once a year, because one person pinned at 95% every month is a resignation waiting to happen, not a star performer.
when: You are pricing a retainer and need to know how many billable hours it must cover to pay for the team behind it.
A month felt full but the profit was thin and you want to see how much of the payroll was actually invoiced.
You are deciding whether to hire, because current utilization shows whether the existing team has spare capacity.
mistakes: Counting every hour worked as billable. Internal meetings, admin and pitching are hours you paid for but cannot invoice.
Chasing 100% utilization. Somewhere near 70-80% is healthy; a team pinned at 95% burns out and churns.
Taking available hours from a 40-hour week when your team actually works 45. The denominator is what you paid for, not what the calendar says.

wc.what: Working capital is the money tied up in running the business day to day: stock on the shelf, plus what customers owe you, minus what you owe suppliers. A business can be profitable and still run out of cash, because profit is an accounting number and working capital is cash. The calculator turns the three lines into one figure and a cycle length, so you can see how many days your money is locked up before it comes back.
wc.formula: Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities. Cash Conversion Cycle = Days Inventory + Days Receivable - Days Payable.
when: You are profitable but the bank account keeps going to zero and you need to see where the money sits.
A customer asks for 60-day terms and you want to price what that costs you.
You are applying for a working-capital limit and need the number a bank will ask for.
mistakes: Counting only stock and forgetting receivables. Slow-paying customers tie up more cash than slow-moving stock.
Treating a negative working capital as always bad. For a subscription business with prepaid plans it is healthy.
Ignoring the cycle length. 50 lakh tied up for 90 days is a very different business from the same amount tied up for 15.

zodiac.what: Your Western zodiac sign is fixed by your birth date and the sun's position on that date, which is why it is the one sign you can look up from a date alone. The twelve signs run on the same calendar every year - Aries starts around 21 March, Cancer around 21 June - with a shift of about a day between leap years. This tool returns the sign for the date you enter and names the exact range it used, so a birthday on a cusp is settled rather than guessed.
zodiac.formula: Each sign owns a fixed band of the calendar: Capricorn runs 22 December to 19 January, Aquarius 20 January to 18 February, Pisces 19 February to 20 March, Aries 21 March to 19 April, Taurus 20 April to 20 May, Gemini 21 May to 20 June, Cancer 21 June to 22 July, Leo 23 July to 22 August, Virgo 23 August to 22 September, Libra 23 September to 22 October, Scorpio 23 October to 21 November, Sagittarius 22 November to 21 December. The tool compares your month and day against these boundaries and returns the sign whose band contains the date.
when: You need your sun sign for a horoscope and have only the date.
A birthday sits on a cusp and you want to know which sign the date alone points to.
You are filling a profile that asks for a zodiac sign and do not want to look up a chart.
mistakes: Reading a cusp birthday as certain. Within a day of a boundary the sign depends on the birth time, not the date.
Using the Western sign for a Vedic question. Rashi uses the moon, not the sun, and needs the birth time.
Assuming the date ranges never move. A leap year pushes the boundaries by about a day.
